papers.title: Crowd dynamics in historical perspective: Reframing the Amritsar massacre through agent-based modelling and social psychology
papers.abstract: Crowds have long held a paradoxical place in the human imagination, feared for their destructive potential yet essential for collective expression. This tension was tragically manifested in the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre, when British colonial troops opened fire on a peaceful gathering in Amritsar, India. Although officially 379 deaths were recorded, eyewitnesses and historians have long challenged this figure. With this study, we critically revisit the events through the lens of the specific role of the crowd as a phenomenon, both regarding the physical and the socio-psychological dynamics. Our agent-based simulations distribute the 1650 rounds that were fired over a crowd trying to leave through the five narrow openings of the documented geometry. They yield numbers of people hit above the official count under every assumption tested: 660 in the lowest case tested, half a hit per round and the smallest crowd, about 1650 for the crowd sizes that eyewitnesses reported, and 2500 at the hits per round that Wagner’s estimate implies. The openings pass at most 5850 people in ten minutes; for any larger crowd the toll is fixed by the rounds fired and the hits per round, whatever the crowd does, and the size and behaviour of the crowd decide only who falls and where: in the queues at the openings, not at the firing line. On the socio-psychological front, we explore how early 20th-century discourses, influenced by Le Bon’s theory of crowd psychology, constructed the crowd as an inherently irrational and threatening entity, thus providing a rationale for the application of excessive force. Our findings show that acknowledging the socio-cultural construction of crowds as a relevant factor in how state power engages with and respond to collective gatherings brings to light contemporary parallels and the risks posed by their rhetorical framing. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of interdisciplinary modelling for both historical accountability and current crowd safety, particularly in an era of growing political unrest, surveillance, and militarised crowd policing.

papers.title: Resilience in crisis and emergency management: the role of performance audit
papers.abstract: Public sector organisations (PSOs) operate in an environment of unprecedented complexity and volatility, facing challenges such as natural disasters, financial and economic fluctuations, and social issues. These complexities strain their capacity to deliver services effectively. Performance audits assess PSOs’ ability to anticipate, plan for, sustain, and recover from crises, strengthening resilience by systematically identifying vulnerabilities and enhancing adaptability. The paper examines PSOs’ actions in Australia and New Zealand during crises and analyses performance audit evaluations and recommendations. Although PSOs responded to the crises, the paper identifies several deficiencies in governance and accountability, procurement and financial management, data integrity and information management, network building, and operational efficiency. Strengthening these areas is essential to enhance organisational resilience, preparedness, and recovery capacity in future crises.

papers.title: Sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers: Implications for biosafety and occupational vaccination – A systematic review with meta-analysis
papers.abstract: This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.

papers.title: Key attributes for industry 4.0–enabled occupational safety and health management in modern methods of construction: a Delphi–VAHP approach
papers.abstract: The adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies presents significant opportunities to enhance occupational safety and health (OSH) management within modern methods of construction (MMC). However, organisations often lack clarity on which factors are crucial for the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies for OSH improvement in MMC. Existing studies have mainly investigated individual technologies, adoption barriers, or organisational capability factors, without systematically identifying and prioritising the comprehensive set of people, organisational, technological, and infrastructure attributes that enable effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC. This study addresses this gap by identifying, validating, and prioritising the key attributes for effective Industry 4.0-enabled OSH management in MMC using a four-stage methodological approach comprising SLR, expert verification, Delphi method, and voting analytic hierarchy process (VAHP). Through a combination of systematic literature review (SLR) and expert verification, 21 attributes were identified and grouped into four clusters: people, organisation, technology, and infrastructure. The 21 identified and validated attributes were then ranked by a group of experts through a two-round Delphi survey. Following this, the weights and importance of attributes were determined using the voting analytical hierarchy process (VAHP). The results indicate that organisation and people clusters achieved the highest relative priorities; Management support, workforce competence, and technology acceptance were identified as the highest-priority attributes. These findings reveal a sociotechnical hierarchy in which organisational and human capabilities are prioritised above technological and infrastructural capabilities, suggesting successful Industry 4.0-enabled transformation for OSH improvement depends more on social-subsystem capability than on technology deployment alone.

papers.title: Cultivating high-reliable organizing: A holistic perspective
papers.abstract: High-reliable organizing (HRO) has long been associated with how organizations sustain reliable performance under conditions of complexity, uncertainty, and change. While Mindful Organizing (MO), and Resilience Engineering (RE) have generated important theoretical insights, guidance on how organizations can cultivate HRO in everyday organizing remains fragmented. This conceptual essay develops a holistic perspective that positions HRO as an ongoing accomplishment rather than a fixed organizational capability or the outcome of implementing isolated concepts. Through a systematic comparison of the five established MO processes and the four resilience potentials, we show how the two perspectives can be related while preserving their distinct analytical orientations. MO focuses on the collective organizing through which people notice, interpret, coordinate, and respond to emerging situations, while RE emphasizes organizational potentials to monitor, respond, anticipate, and learn under changing conditions. Building on this synthesis, we develop the holistic framework of HRO, identify two additional organizing processes— preoccupation with things that go right and self-awareness —and develop an approach to cultivating and operationalizing HRO through collaborative inquiry, driving forces, and situated practices. Rather than prescribing predefined practices, we argue that organizations can cultivate mindsets and directions of attention that guide how established concepts are translated to context-sensitive action while remaining grounded in the scientific foundations of HRO, MO, and RE. The essay contributes a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding and cultivating high-reliable organizing as an ongoing accomplishment in complex sociotechnical systems.

papers.title: A systems analysis of fatal railway level crossing crashes
papers.abstract: Fatal railway level crossing crashes represent a public safety challenge. Existing data on these crashes is limited, mostly focusing on frequencies rather than providing an in-depth understanding of the underlying causes. This study aimed to demonstrate the utility of using coronial findings, supplemented with reports from investigation agencies, to understand the system-wide factors contributing to railway crossing crashes and to explore the proposed recommendations. A systems thinking accident analysis approach, the AcciMap technique, underpinned the analysis. Over a 20-year period, 151 cases were identified, involving a range of road user types. Of these cases, 135 included sufficient detail to extract contributory factors and recommendations. A total of 483 contributory factors were extracted and used to develop an aggregate AcciMap. Most factors were associated with road user behaviour and/or individual characteristics, as opposed to systemic issues. Unique contributory factors were identified for crashes occurring at active crossings (those with dynamic warnings present) versus passive crossings (those with signage only). A total of 184 recommendations were extracted and mapped using the AcciMap framework. Recommendations tended to take a system-wide view of preventing future occurrences, acknowledging the complexity of managing risk at the interface of two transport modes. The analysis provided important information to support crash prevention efforts, including a set of common systemic recommendations identified from the data that require collaborative efforts across road and rail stakeholders. Mechanisms for supporting this collaboration should be further explored. The study also provided learnings regarding the nature of coronial investigations and areas for potential improvement.

papers.title: Safety in military organizations –A scoping review
papers.abstract: Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have been extensively studied in military contexts. However, existing research is often fragmented, focusing narrowly on climate metrics or individual subdomains, thereby overlooking deeper structural and cultural dynamics. There is a need to integrate findings across studies to better understand how these concepts interrelate and drive effective safety in a military context. This systematic literature review synthesizes findings from 28 empirical studies to better understand how safety is enacted and sustained across individual, group, and organizational levels in military organizations. The findings include critical enablers of effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe learning environments. While safety climate assessments are frequently used to gauge perceptions of safety, overreliance on such tools may obscure power dynamics, cultural norms, and systemic constraints that affect frontline behavior. A recurring challenge across the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices required in real-world operations—particularly in combat or high-risk scenarios. Safety in military contexts must also be understood as a dynamic and integrated process, where leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to shape behavior. The findings support a shift from compliance-focused models toward more flexible, learning-oriented approaches. Future research should address current gaps, including the limited focus on gender dynamics, team-level processes, and longitudinal designs capable of capturing change over time and across operational contexts.

papers.title: Organizational safety and adaptive work practices in aquaculture
papers.abstract: The aquaculture industry is marked by considerable operational variability stemming from shifting environmental conditions, biological processes, and complex work activities. While prior research has focused primarily on technical safety, fish welfare, and formal safety management, less attention has been paid to how workers manage variability in everyday practice. This qualitative single-case study examines organizational variability in a Norwegian salmon-farming company by addressing two research questions: (1) How do aquaculture workers manage variability in their daily safety practices? and (2) How do local work practices influence organizational safety? The empirical material comprises documents and nine semi-structured interviews with operational and managerial personnel. The analysis draws on both safety theories and organizational learning perspectives. The findings show that workers manage variability through adaptive work practices grounded in practical experience, teamwork, and continuous adjustment to changing environmental and operational conditions, rather than through strict adherence to formal procedures. Local work practices influence organizational safety by creating and sustaining safety knowledge within stable communities of practice, where newcomers gradually develop the competence and judgment needed to work safely. Although formal safety management systems provide an important framework, their effectiveness depends on how well they are integrated with everyday operational practice. Rapid organizational growth challenges existing learning processes by making practical safety knowledge harder to transfer and sustain. The findings demonstrate that organizational safety is achieved not only through formal safety management systems but also through adaptive work practices and the social processes that enable workers to manage operational variability.

papers.title: Transitioning from traditional hospital design to activity-based care: A longitudinal case study of differential occupational health and safety consequences across clinical settings and professional roles
papers.abstract: The activity-based care (ABC) model, adapted from activity-based offices, has emerged as a new approach to healthcare facility design. Evidence on its consequences for occupational health and safety-relevant outcomes remains limited. The study examines how transitioning from a traditional hospital design to the ABC model is associated with changes in employee experiences of task–environment alignment and psychosocial work environment, self-reported health, sick leave and turnover over time, and differences in changes across professional roles and clinic types. A repeated-measures survey was conducted in an outpatient hospital unit across 10 specialised clinics. Data were collected 3 months before relocation and at 6 and 18 months post-relocation. Generalised least-squares models examined change over time and tested interactions with professional role and clinic type. Sick leave and turnover were analysed over approximately 1 year before and after relocation using segmented interrupted time-series regression. Ratings of task–environment alignment varied across clinic types and professional roles. Consultation-based clinics and physicians and administrative employees showed persistent declines over time, while surgical/radiology clinics and nursing roles remained stable or improved. Stress and recovery indicators worsened similarly across all groups. Psychosocial conditions were stable, though job satisfaction, perceived quality of work and referral intentions declined. Turnover remained unchanged, while sick leave varied across contexts and roles. The consequences of ABC implementation are not uniform but depend on the alignment of the redesigned workspace and the task demands of different clinical settings and professional groups, a contingency that cannot be easily detected with single time-point post-occupancy evaluation.

papers.title: Healthy crew, healthy life: The captain’s role in commercial fishing crew health
papers.abstract: Objectives Commercial fishermen engage in one of the most dangerous professions in the United States. This qualitative study explored how the internal priorities of commercial fishermen captains influence the health and well-being of their crew members. Methods Data were collected via semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted under the 2025 Southeast and Gulf Coast Fishing First Aid and Safety Training program. Commercial fishermen and individuals working adjacent to the industry (n = 10) were recruited using purposive sampling. Using a priori qualitative coding, two coders performed a thematic analysis using ATLAS.ti. Results Overall, participants reported that crew health and wellness were affected by the captain’s attitudes. Participants (40%) explored crew preparedness as a central theme in captains’ approaches to crew well-being, with the captain’s knowledge of pre-existing conditions allowing for a proactive approach to medication management and injury/illness reduction (30%). Some (20%) highlighted a conflict of priorities between crew productivity and well-being or observed that captains’ attitudes towards zero-tolerance policy against substance use would influence substance use onboard the vessel (20%). Conclusion Preparing captains and crew members with safety knowledge and skills can mitigate predictable hazards. These findings highlight the importance of continued research and programming surrounding proactive health management among commercial fishermen captains.

papers.title: Are airbag vests effective in reducing thoracoabdominal injuries in motorcycle crashes? An epidemiological perspective
papers.abstract: Background Powered two-wheeler riders are disproportionately exposed to serious and fatal injuries in road crashes, trunk trauma representing a major contributor to this burden. Wearable airbags have been developed to mitigate impact forces on the trunk. We aimed to assess the effectiveness of inflated airbag vests in reducing the risk of trunk injuries among motorcyclists involved in real-world crashes. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study combining two datasets of crash-involved motorcyclists: the EDAIR survey, targeting airbag users, with self-reported crash circumstances and injuries; and the SECU2RM survey, with self-reported crash circumstances and injuries extracted from linked trauma registry. EDAIR riders equipped with an inflated airbag vest during the crash were compared to riders without or with non-inflated airbag from EDAIR ( internal analysis) and SECU2RM ( external analysis). Health outcomes included thoracoabdominal injuries (TAI) and serious TAI. Risk ratios were estimated using log-binomial regression with propensity score weighting. Results Inflated airbag vest was associated with a 50% lower risk of TAI in the internal analysis (N = 764, RR = 0.50, 95%CI: 0.35–0.68) and a 37% lower risk in the external analysis (N = 853, RR = 0.63, 95%CI: 0.43–0.93). Associations with serious TAI were inconclusive. Conclusion This study provides the first real-world evaluation of airbag vest effectiveness. Despite distinct study populations and sources of bias, both analyses exhibited protective associations between inflated airbag and thoracoabdominal injury risk, consistent with biomechanical evidence. These findings support potential public health value of airbag vests. Larger-scale studies with improved crash kinetics and rider’s characterization are warranted to confirm these findings.

papers.title: Identifying a dynamic information trading zone framework via insights from full-scale emergency exercises
papers.abstract: The article examines how the co-creation of a Common Operational Picture (COP) in multi-actor crisis response operations can be understood through the concept of Information Trading Zones (ITZ). The analysis is grounded in the theory of Situation Awareness (SA), including Endsley’s conceptualisation of individual, Team SA and Shared SA, and draws on Galison’s notion of trading zones as intercalation, the insertion of an intermediate concept or mechanism to bridge existing explanatory levels. In this study, ITZ is introduced as an intercalating construct linking information exchange, sensemaking, and coordinated action. Drawing on extensive qualitative analyses of five full-scale crisis exercises, the study traces the evolution of an operational framework that conceptualises ITZ as both a precondition for and an integral component of the co-creation of a COP. Within this framework, ITZ are positioned as socio-technical spaces where information is negotiated, interpreted, and stabilised across organisational boundaries, enabling the development of Shared and Team SA in the face of uncertainty. The article offers concrete recommendations for both researchers and practice, outlining how the interplay among ITZ, COP, and SA can inform the design of information systems that more effectively support coordination, sense-making, and decision-making in Emergency Management contexts.

papers.title: Rural occupational health in Colombia: policy–practice gaps among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca
papers.abstract: This research article examines disparities in health protection and promotion policies for rural workers, using as a case study the municipality of Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. The study adopts a multi-method approach that articulates qualitative and quantitative tools. In the qualitative phase, 14 interviews and 2 focus groups were conducted with key actors at the local, departmental and national levels, including workers, employers and government representatives. A survey adapted from the ILO Vision Zero Fund was applied, with a sample of 200 agricultural workers and an analysis of 41 relevant variables.The results show persistent deficiencies in the mechanisms for the prevention of occupational risks, in the coverage of health services and in information systems needed to adequately characterize rural working conditions. These limitations deepen the precariousness and economic vulnerability of workers, particularly in informal contexts where regulations are scarce or ineffective. We also identify weak institutional coordination that prevents the formulation of public policies adjusted to the territorial realities.The study highlights the need for comprehensive and contextualized policies that recognize the specificities of rural work and promote safer work environments. Differential approaches, including gender sensitivity and local knowledge, are essential to close the gap between regulatory frameworks and the concrete experiences of rural workers. By making these tensions visible, this work aims to provide elements for the construction of inclusive strategies for health promotion in rural areas.

papers.title: Safety concepts through a memetic lens
papers.abstract: Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice.

papers.title: How media narratives shape public sentiment toward electric micromobility: Stronger effects for e-scooters than e-bikes
papers.abstract: Public sentiment toward electric micromobility, particularly e-scooters and e-bikes, is increasingly shaping safety debates and regulatory responses; yet, these attitudes and perceptions have not been systematically evaluated within a unified framework, nor is it clear to what extent they reflect stable judgments versus sensitivity to external narratives. This study addresses these gaps by quantifying public sentiment toward e-bikes and e-scooters and evaluating their responsiveness to controlled negative media narrative exposure. A unified survey framework was developed to enable consistent evaluation, combining statement-based measures with image-based scenario assessments. Two complementary studies were conducted with Australian participants. Study 1 (N = 1027) established baseline sentiment in the absence of media exposure, and Study 2 (N = 1025) examined how responses shift following controlled exposure to negative news headlines. The results showed that public sentiment is multi-dimensional and mixed. While both modes received moderate recognition in terms of sustainability and legitimacy, practical acceptance remained lower, particularly for e-scooters. Exposure to negative media narratives produced broader and more consistent shifts toward less favorable sentiments for e-scooters, especially in perceptions of rider behavior and public-space interaction, whereas e-bike responses remained comparatively stable and more robust to media narrative exposure. In contrast, evaluations of concrete negative situations showed no systematic change following exposure, indicating that these evaluations are grounded in situational interpretation rather than external framing. The findings suggest that public sentiment should be used cautiously to inform policy development. While consistent concerns linked to observable safety issues justify targeted interventions, broader sentiment shifts may reflect narrative influence rather than actual conditions. Effective policy should therefore be informed not only by public sentiment but also by objective evidence on behavior, exposure, and risk.

papers.title: A longitudinal comparison of shared and private e-scooter crashes, near-miss rates, attributions and characteristics
papers.abstract: As e-scooters have become increasingly common in urban areas, safety concerns have grown. However, most safety research does not distinguish between shared and private e-scooter use. Moreover, no studies have examined within-person changes in safety outcomes over time. This study followed Australian e-scooter riders (n = 285) across two survey waves conducted 12 months apart (follow-up and final) and comprised two analyses. First, we compared riders’ most recent near misses and crashes on shared and private e-scooters in terms of their characteristics and riders’ attributions. At follow-up, 32.7% of participants were private-only riders, 51.2% shared-only, and 16.1% mixed-use. Most near misses involved another road user (78.1% at follow-up, 70.1% at final), while a substantial share of crashes did not (55.6%, 59.1%). Private e-scooters accounted for the majority of near misses involving another road user at both waves (64.0%, 76.6%). Near misses occurring on shared e-scooters were consistently attributed to riders’ own lack of experience. Second, we modelled within-person changes in near-miss rates. A Poisson generalised linear mixed model, with a random intercept for participant and riding exposure as an offset, tested whether near-miss rate changed between waves, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Near-miss rate did not differ significantly between waves. Riders outside Queensland and Victoria had a lower rate than Queensland riders (IRR = 0.27). Riders with primary/secondary or bachelor’s degree education were associated with lower rates than those with post-school qualifications. Riders’ attribution of shared e-scooter incidents to inexperience suggests onboarding and practical training warrant further evaluation.

papers.title: The role of personal norms in farmers’ safety practices: Protective equipment use in pesticide handling
papers.abstract: Farmers’ use of personal protective equipment (PPE) during pesticide handling has been studied, but factors shaping this behavior can vary considerably. Farmers’ intention to use PPE in pesticide handling and observed protective behavior were studied using the norm activation model (NAM). Data analysis was conducted using descriptive statistics, Spearman’s correlation, multiple linear regression, and binary logistic regression models. Almost fifty-nine (58.9%) of farmers showed unsafe behavior regarding PPE use. Intention to use PPE was low (mean: 2.415 on a 1–5 scale) and positively associated with observed protective behavior. Regarding NAM constructs, farmers showed moderate personal norms (mean: 3.027), slightly lower awareness of the consequences associated with not using PPE (mean: 2.888), and relatively weak ascription of responsibility (mean: 2.741) for reducing those consequences. Personal norms significantly predicted both intention and observed protective behavior (P < 0.01). In turn, awareness of consequences and ascription of responsibility were significant positive predictors of personal norms, supporting the applicability of NAM for understanding PPE-related behavior. Further analysis indicated that personal norms were negatively associated with age and farm size (P < 0.01), suggesting weaker norms among older farmers and those managing larger farms. Conversely, education was positively correlated with personal norms (P < 0.01). Overall, personal norms played a central role in shaping PPE use, with their relationship influenced by recognition of the risks of non-use and acceptance of responsibility for mitigating them. Enhancing communication about pesticide risks and emphasizing the importance of PPE may help strengthen personal norms and promote safer PPE-related practices.

papers.title: Safety and health of workers in post-disaster reconstruction: a scoping review and evidence map
papers.abstract: Post-disaster reconstruction (PDR) is essential for restoring damaged communities, yet the occupational safety and health (OSH) of PDR workers remains poorly understood. Although PDR involves many familiar construction hazards, these risks arise under distinct conditions, including damaged infrastructure, compressed recovery timelines, environmental contamination, fragmented governance, and pressure for visible recovery. This scoping review and evidence map examined peer-reviewed and authoritative gray literature on OSH among PDR workers. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, the review used a Population-Concept-Context framework to search bibliographic databases and targeted organizational sources for English-language literature published from 2005 to 2025. The final evidence base included 55 sources, comprising 40 peer-reviewed publications and 15 gray literature documents. The review identified a geographically uneven and thematically concentrated evidence base, with strong representation from the United States and multi-country sources, and greater attention to multi-hazard and earthquake-related contexts than to other disaster types. Findings show that PDR workers face overlapping OSH hazards and exposures. Evidence was strongest for early recovery tasks such as debris removal, demolition, and cleanup, while later reconstruction phases, informal labor, volunteers, undocumented workers, and self-recovery residents remained underexamined. The review also highlights major methodological, policy, and practice gaps, including limited longitudinal evidence, inconsistent outcome measures, weak surveillance, and insufficient worker-specific protections. By integrating peer-reviewed and gray literature, this review frames PDR as a distinct OSH context and develops Faster Reconstruction Syndrome as a concept, interpreted through Job Demands-Resources and safety-climate theory to explain how recovery-speed pressures may weaken worker protection in disaster recovery policy and practice.
papers.citation_text: Solomon Sesesie Ajasa, Patrick Shane Crawford. Safety and health of workers in post-disaster reconstruction: a scoping review and evidence map[J]. Safety Science, 2027, 206: 107505. DOI: 10.1016/j.ssci.2026.107505.

papers.title: From precarious work to occupational health outcomes in hotel housekeepers: a narrative review with meta-synthesis
papers.abstract: Introduction: Hotel housekeepers sustain the core functioning of the hospitality industry yet perform demanding, repetitive, and undervalued work associated with substantial physical and psychosocial risks. Understanding how working conditions shape health, motivation, and lived experience is essential for informing prevention strategies and promoting decent work. Methods A sequential narrative review and qualitative meta -synthesis were conducted to integrate and reinterpret evidence across disciplines and study designs. Searches covered five academic databases and gray literature without year or language limits. Studies were screened using predefined criteria, appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools, and synthesized through narrative, tabular, and meta -analytical thematic analysis, with findings interpreted through the JD-R framework. Results Findings revealed employment precarity, work intensification, musculoskeletal pain, chemical and biological hazards, and elevated stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Time pressure fostered coping strategies such as skipping meals and delaying bathroom use. Gendered labor divisions, discrimination, and negative supervision contributed to invisibility and limited autonomy. Workers also expressed pride, intrinsic motivation, and collective action to make their contributions visible. Conclusions This review demonstrates that housekeeping is characterized by structural precarity and cumulative health burdens alongside resilience and emerging activism. Improving occupational health requires organizational and policy transformations: realistic workloads, safer equipment, secure contracts, participatory risk management, and leadership practices grounded in dignity and fairness; rather than reliance on individual coping. Structural change is essential to advance safer, more equitable, and sustainable workplaces in the hospitality sector. The JD-R framework highlights the need to reduce demand and strengthen resources.

papers.title: Systemic approaches in human factors and ergonomics for analysing team dynamics: A systematic review
papers.abstract: Team dynamics in complex sociotechnical systems are critical for safety and organisational effectiveness. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the utility and applicability of systemic Human Factors and Ergonomics(HFE) approaches for analysing team dynamics. Four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect) were searched for peer-reviewed articles published in English between 2020 and September 2025. Studies were included if they applied systemic HFE methods to analyse team dynamics in organisational settings. Studies focusing solely on individual performance or lacking methodological detail were excluded. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data, and methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Data were synthesised using thematic analysis. Seventy-seven studies were included, with healthcare being the most represented domain (n = 39). Most studies (51.9%) used adapted or combined approaches. Communication and coordination were the most frequently analysed dimensions of team dynamics. Established frameworks (e.g., SEIPS, FRAM) supported system-level analysis, while author-developed methods provided greater insight into local interactions. Hybrid approaches enabled integration across levels of analysis. Most studies were of high methodological quality (64.9%). These patterns informed a two-axis model positioning systemic HFE approaches by level of analysis and methodological integration, operationalised as a framework for method selection. Systemic HFE approaches are effective for analysing team dynamics in complex settings; however, no single method is universally optimal. Effectiveness depends on alignment between the analytical approach, context, and research objectives. Hybrid and adapted approaches appearing particularly promising. Further research is needed in underrepresented domains and through comparative methodological studies.

papers.title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
papers.abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. The findings invite policymakers promoting stakeholder engagement and stakeholder diversity as strategies in risk management and crisis response to critically reflect about the mechanisms through which such engagement can be effectively fostered.

papers.title: Workplace responses to perpetration of family and domestic violence: a global scoping review
papers.abstract: Introduction Family and domestic violence (FDV), which includes intimate partner and family violence, affects workplace safety through spillover impacts on workers, organisations, and occupational health systems. To date, workplace interventions addressing the issue of FDV have predominantly concentrated on providing support to victim-survivors, while there is limited research regarding employer responses to employees who perpetrate such violence. Method A scoping review was conducted following Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidelines, which examined existing evidence from workplace policies, practices, and organisational mechanisms addressing FDV perpetration by workers. Peer-reviewed studies and high-quality grey literature on workplace responses to perpetration of FDV were systematically searched across multiple databases and online sources, and 28 documents on workplace responses to FDV perpetration were analysed. Results Findings from the scoping review reveal four dominant insights across the literature: 1. Perpetration of FDV is a major workplace problem, yet responses are under-researched; 2. Workplaces employ wide-ranging and varied responses, from zero tolerance dismissal of perpetrators to responsibility avoidance; 3. Responses lack a solid evidence-base and regulatory frameworks to address the problem remain weak; 4. Practical strategies are provided to better manage risk, strengthen safety, and reduce violence. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for clearer organisational guidance, evidence-based strategies, and robust regulatory frameworks to strengthen workplace responses to FDV perpetration and improve occupational safety outcomes. Practical applications Effective workplace responses to perpetration of FDV should consider work design factors, referral pathways and confidentiality protections which are guided by graduated accountability models and regulatory frameworks.

papers.title: Lifecycle costs of safety instrumented systems in process industries: a systematic literature review
papers.abstract: A safety instrumented system (SIS) is an automated system designed to detect and mitigate potential risk of hazardous conditions in industrial processes by taking actions to prevent or mitigate incidents. It is essential because it helps protect people, equipment, and the environment by reducing the risk of accidents in hazardous operations, such as in chemical plants, oil refineries, or power stations. While the primary objective of SIS design is safety, economic considerations, particularly lifecycle cost, play a pivotal role in decision-making during the design phase. Although research efforts exist to incorporate lifecycle cost with safety, the literature is fragmented and lacks a comprehensive lifecycle cost framework. Therefore, a systematic literature review is conducted to uncover safety instrumented systems’ lifecycle cost elements and the decision variables that impact them. The review results lead to a comprehensive and structured cost calculation framework to assess SIS designed to protect a process unit economically. Finally, this study provides perspectives on potential research directions relevant to SIS lifecycle cost, including the impact of systematic failures, cybersecurity integration, the relative weighting of different cost elements, inclusion of risk costs, and various SIS application types.

papers.title: The safety and health plan for construction works: preventive planning tool or mere formal compliance
papers.abstract: The construction sector is characterized by high organizational complexity derived from its temporary, dynamic, and process-specific nature. This industry registers some of the highest occupational accident rates worldwide. Within the European regulatory framework, Directive 92/57/EEC establishes the Health and Safety Plan (H&SP) as the principal instrument for preventive management on-site. In Spain, the transposition of this Directive introduced a preliminary design-phase document (Health and Safety Study or Basic Study, H&SS/H&SBS), intended to identify risks and define preventive measures that subsequently inform the contractor’s H&SP. Despite the importance of H&SS/H&SBS documents within the safety management process, empirical evidence remains limited regarding both their technical quality and their predictive capacity to explain the quality of subsequent H&SPs. This study addresses this gap through a qualitative and quantitative approach aimed at evaluating the intrinsic quality of H&SS/H&SBS and H&SP documents and modelling the dependency relationship between them. A database comprising 560 documents (280 H&SS/H&SBS and 280 H&SP) from 280 construction projects was assessed using a Delphi-based expert evaluation tool combined with a ratio weighting method. The results reveal consistently low levels of document quality and a limited capacity of H&SS/H&SBS to predict the quality of the corresponding H&SP. These findings suggest a systemic “cascade” failure in preventive planning, whereby documents frequently operate as instruments of formal compliance rather than as effective safety management tools. Our models’ findings support the need for effective audits and advanced technical training for professionals drafting these documents to improve preventive planning.

papers.title: Polycentric risk governance across safety and security risk logics
papers.abstract: The regulatory regime governing the Norwegian petroleum sector changed significantly in response to new geopolitical conditions following the war in Ukraine and the sabotage of the Nord Stream I and II pipelines. New legal security requirements and security risk logics were introduced into a sector whose traditional regulatory regime and risk logic had been intrinsically oriented toward safety. This shift altered the balance between safety and security considerations within the sector. This article explores the implications for regulatory regimes and risk logics when transitioning from safety-oriented to security-oriented regulatory models. Our ambition is primarily conceptual and theoretical, with the Norwegian petroleum industry serving as an illustrative case. The article analyses the emerging interface between safety and security, emphasizing the ontological, epistemological, and procedural divergences that complicate the integration of security concerns − focused on intentional, adversarial threats − into established safety regimes that manage unintentional harm. Anchored in a polycentric governance framework, the article examines how geopolitical developments have created tensions between rule-based and risk-based regulatory models, and the implications for organizational practices, regulatory oversight, and tripartite cooperation. It concludes by proposing a model of enforced self-regulation that reconciles safety and security logics, highlighting the need for adaptive, resilient, and knowledge-driven approaches to risk management in complex and evolving threat landscapes.

papers.title: The viral deviation: a quantitative analysis of social media engagement metrics on non-compliant flight deck behaviors
papers.abstract: Background Normalization of Deviance (NoD) is a well-documented organizational failure mode in aviation, yet its propagation through digital ecosystems remains unexplored. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) highlights a critical mentorship vacuum due to pilot retirements, and social media platforms increasingly serve as informal training environments. This study introduces the concept of Algorithmic Normalization of Deviance- ANoD, hypothesizing that recommendation algorithms systematically reward and amplify “gray-zone” cockpit behaviors that erode sterile flight deck protocols. Method We conducted a stratified netnographic analysis of 150 high-visibility aviation videos (N = 150) across Instagram Reels, split between algorithmically recommended content (n = 100) and curated influencer content (n = 50). A novel coding framework operationalized compliance (Compliant vs. Gray Zone vs. Deviant) and incentive structures. Engagement metrics were analyzed to quantify the algorithmic advantage of non-compliant behavior. Results The analysis reveals a directionally consistent “Viral Deviation” pattern rather than a statistically decisive one. Gray-zone recordings (i.e., technically legal but procedurally borderline) comprised 57% of the sample and attracted higher engagement than compliant content, although this difference was small and did not reach conventional significance (d = 0.24, p = 0.11). The clearest signal emerged between content sources: algorithmically surfaced posts showed significantly higher interaction rates than curated influencer posts (d = 0.31, p = 0.029), a small but statistically significant per-view advantage for content promoted directly by the recommendation system. Structural incentive analysis further indicates that monetization pressures co-occur with increased gray-zone production, structurally analogous to a parallel, shadow curriculum associated with conditions that may facilitate drift. Conclusion The study identifies statistical associations, not causal relationships, and the downstream behavioural impact on pilots is hypothesised from the algorithmic-pattern evidence rather than directly measured. Within those bounds, social media algorithms constitute a structurally unmonitored distribution channel whose observed associations with gray-zone content amplification are consistent with a normalisation-of-deviance feedback mechanism operating beyond current regulatory oversight — an association that warrants urgent empirical validation and proactive governance. We propose a shift from prohibition to risk-stratified governance, recommending that regulators distinguish between handheld (high-risk) and mounted (managed-risk) devices, and integrate digital algorithmic literacy into ab-initio pilot training to counter this new systemic threat.

papers.title: Mapping the Scientific Landscape of Boilover in Industrial Storage Tank Fires: A Combined Bibliometric and Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Boilover is a destructive phenomenon that occurs during a fire in hydrocarbon tanks with a bottom layer of water; it is characterised by an explosive eruption of burning fuel and a sudden increase in thermal radiation. Despite research conducted since the 1950s, our understanding of this phenomenon remains fragmentary, with a limited body of scientific literature (118 publications indexed in Scopus between 1959 and 2025) and a lack of validation at an industrial scale. To address these limitations, this study combines bibliometric analysis with a systematic literature review to analyse the evolution of boilover research and synthesise current knowledge of the phenomenon's mechanisms, experimental investigations, analytical and numerical modelling approaches, and the main factors influencing its development. The bibliometric analysis examines the dynamics of scientific output, collaboration networks and the thematic structure of the field, whilst the systematic review identifies the main scientific findings, the limitations of current knowledge and the key research gaps. The results highlight a high concentration of scientific impact centred on pioneering work, a division of the field into several distinct areas (combustion, process safety and risk management), and a persistent fragmentation of collaborations. The review further shows that, despite significant progress in understanding boilover mechanisms and developing analytical and numerical models, large-scale experimental validation remains limited, predictive capabilities remain insufficient, and several scientific challenges persist, particularly concerning emulsified crude oils, wall effects and scaling phenomena. This review therefore highlights the main scientific gaps and proposes several research priorities to improve understanding, prediction, and prevention of the boilover phenomenon. papers.title: Risk Analysis of Combustible Cladding in Proximity to Vehicles
papers.abstract: Building façade fires resulting from the ignition of combustible cladding materials have been reported extensively. However, research specifically addressing the risk posed by external fire sources, such as vehicles parked near cladding, is still limited. This study applies probabilistic analysis to assess fire risks associated with car fires in proximity to combustible cladding, considering Aluminium Composite Panels (ACP) containing a polymer-based core and Expanded Polystyrene (EPS). The influence of wind conditions is incorporated into the analysis. The objective is to create a database supporting decision-making on rectification measures, reducing façade fire risks, and ensuring occupant safety. This study is developed within Cladding Safety Victoria’s framework for mitigating fire risks.

papers.title: Interpretable Machine Learning Models for Predicting Compressive Strength of Binary Blended Geopolymer Concrete Exposed to Elevated Temperatures
papers.abstract: Predicting the strength of geopolymer concrete (GPC) after fire incidents is crucial for ensuring structural safety. From this lens, the present study investigates the prediction capabilities of machine learning (ML) algorithms to examine the residual strength of GPC after being subjected to the ISO 834 fire curve. More specifically, a comprehensive dataset from fire experiments comprising of ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS), fly ash (FA), sodium hydroxide (SH), sodium silicate (SS), alkaline activator to binder (AAS/B) ratio, molarity (M), extra water (EW), curing temperature (T), exposure to elevated temperature (ET) and exposure time (t) was collected and analyzed. This dataset is utilized to train and test six ML models, namely, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Categorial Boosting (CatBoost), Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), and Gradient Boosting (GB). The models were trained via a cross-validation process and then examined using statistical indicators. In comparison with all the ML models, CatBoost shows the highest accuracy with an R2 of 0.997 and the lowest RMSE value. To further enhance the developed models, their interpretability was examined using SHAP, which shows that t, T, and ET were the most influential factors that govern the strength of the GPC mix. This finding highlights the potential of ML in developing light and cost-efficient prediction frameworks for post-fire assessment of binary blended GPC to help augment the specialized and expensive nature of fire testing.

papers.title: High-Temporal-Resolution Long-Term Prediction Model for Fire Temperature Field of Timber Arch Lounge Bridges Based on Spatiotemporal Attention
papers.abstract: Fires inflict substantial losses of life and property annually, posing a severe threat to global cultural heritage, particularly wooden structures such as timber arch lounge bridges. Timber arch lounge bridges, also known as Chinese covered timber bridges or covered bridges, feature complex fire spread dynamics, which poses a challenge to the accuracy and real-time capability of fire prediction technology. However, existing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation methods, when applied to timber arch lounge bridges, are computationally expensive and impractical for real-time applications. To address these challenges, this study proposed a fire prediction fusion framework with high temporal resolution and long-term forecasting capability based on spatiotemporal attention mechanisms. First, the sparsity prediction module generates a sparse sequence through recurrent iterative operations. Subsequently, the interpolation module interpolates the missing values to form a complete prediction sequence. The fusion framework demonstrated enhanced long-term prediction performance across both timber arch lounge bridge and closed-building layouts compared to the baselines. Moreover, the fusion framework achieves a 36-fold speed increase over conventional CFD methods in timber arch lounge bridge layouts, indicating its performance advantage. While the current model is trained and validated under a specific fire scenario, these results suggest that the proposed framework has the potential to provide a high-accuracy real-time fire prediction method for emergency management and fire-fighting rescue.

papers.title: Data-Driven Selection of Parametric and Travelling Fire Models for Performance-based Fire Design
papers.abstract: Selecting appropriate design fire models remains a key unresolved challenge in performance-based structural fire engineering, where the applicability of the Eurocode EN 1991-1-2 parametric fire curve and travelling fire (TF) models is not clearly defined. This study proposes a quantitative threshold for selecting between the EN and TF models based on full-scale experimental results. A total of 222 available full-scale natural fire experiments are summarised and used as benchmark data. For each experiment, average compartment fire temperature–time curves are predicted using the EN and TF models, respectively, and their predictive accuracy is quantitatively assessed to determine the best-performing model for each fire test. A logistic regression (LR) model is then derived from the available dataset to predict the best-performing model for a given set of fire inputs. As the required TF model inputs, namely the peak fire temperature, heat release rate per unit area, and fire spread rate, were not reported in the experimental data, a sensitivity study is conducted to evaluate their influence on the derived LR model. The results show that the LR model is most sensitive to the assumed fire spread rate. Therefore, three applicability segments are introduced into the LR model to cover a wider range of fire scenarios. The proposed LR model achieves an average training accuracy of 0.736 and an ROC–AUC of 0.808. A probabilistic risk assessment case study using Monte Carlo simulation demonstrates that the proposed LR model reduces both over- and under-design compared with EN-only or TF-only methods, providing a more balanced and reliable framework for current performance-based structural fire design.

papers.title: Flammability and Feasibility Analysis of Mixture Refrigerants Consisting of R1243zf, RE170, and Flame Retardants (R13I1, R134a, or R125)
papers.abstract: Burning velocity is one of the fundamental flammability parameters, and the maximum burning velocity is a crucial criterion of flammability classification of refrigerants. In this study, an experimental system for measuring the burning velocity of low-carbon flammable gases was established based on ISO standard 817. The combustion reactions of mixture refrigerants consisting of R1243zf, RE170 and flame retardants (R13I1, R134a, or R125) were experimentally investigated. In addition, a combustion reaction kinetic model applicable to R1243zf and its mixtures was established, consisting of 178 species and 1442 elementary reactions. The modified kinetic mechanism reproduced the ISO 817 vertical-tube-derived burning-velocity dataset for R1243zf and its mixtures with a mean deviation of 14.5%. This comparison is regarded as a method-specific benchmark rather than a complete validation of the unstretched adiabatic laminar burning velocity. From the perspective of the thermodynamic properties, flammability and global warming potential (GWP), R1243zf/R13I1/R134a and R1243zf/R13I1/R125 revealed the better flexible in composition proportions optimization since which own sizable zones of Class A1 (as per ASHRAE standard 34) and GWP100< 150 concurrently. Further, based on theoretical calculations, the performance and coefficient of performance (COP) of 20 representative mixtures were evaluated, and the candidate blend compositions identified through preliminary thermodynamic, environmental, and flammability screening were proposed accordingly to meet the application requirements in an air conditioning system.

papers.title: Experimental study of temperature evolution and flame ejection inside a double-opening enclosure
papers.abstract: This article studied the temperature evolution and flame ejection of enclosure fires with the upper and lower openings. Experiments were conducted inside a reduced-scale enclosure with the side length of 0.4 m, which has two openings of the same size, vertically distributed and separated at a distance. Temperature inside the enclosure and flame behavior were recorded for different window sizes, heat release rates and opening separation distances. Result shows that: (1) Temperature inside enclosure rises as total HRR increases, and falls as the opening separation distance increases. This is because air flow rate entering the enclosure increases with the increase of opening separation distance. (2) Critical HRR of ejection rises as the window size increases, and decreases as the increase of opening separation distance. This is because that when the upper opening position is higher, flames are more likely to eject out from the opening after reaching the enclosure top. (3) A normalized separation distance was proposed, which well characterized the effect of separation distance on inside temperature and flame ejection, and the temperature and critical flame ejection were correlated well by the normalized distance. This study for the first time revealed the temperature evolution and flame ejection inside a double-opening enclosure, analyzed the effect of opening separation distance, and proposed the models to quantify the inside temperature and critical HRR for flame ejection, which would make a significant contribution in the theory of building fire dynamics.

papers.title: Effects of State of Charge on Fire Characteristics and Smoke Spread in 18,650 Lithium-Ion Batteries in a Tunnel
papers.abstract: In this work, the combustion dynamics and smoke spread behavior of 18,650 lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) with varying states of charge (SOC: 25%–100%) were experimentally investigated in a model-scale tunnel. The results show that the fire evolution of LIBs can be divided into three stages: initial ignition, intermittent combustion characterized by repeated burst combustion and jet-fire events, and combustion decay. SOC strongly influenced the thermal hazard intensity; the peak flame temperature increased with SOC and reached 1081.4 °C at 100% SOC. The smoke movement during LIB fires exhibited several typical stages, including initial plume formation, ceiling impingement and radial diffusion, smoke stratification with longitudinal propagation, and repeated jet-induced smoke accumulation. The intermittent jet-fire behavior generated multiple high-momentum pulses that transferred kinetic energy to the smoke layer and locally re-accelerated the longitudinal spread. A local velocity increase of 14.6%–40.4% was observed between adjacent measuring points, and this short-term re-acceleration was more pronounced at higher SOCs and near the fire source. These results reveal the coupling between SOC, intermittent jet-fire behavior, and smoke spread dynamics, providing useful insights for smoke control and safety management in tunnel fires involving lithium-ion batteries.

papers.title: When the Cable Insulation Burns: Experimental and 2D Modeling Study of Cables with Flame-Retardant Sheaths and Flammable Insulation
papers.abstract: The integration of flame-retardant (FR) materials into electrical cables mitigates fire hazards; however, the widespread industrial practice of pairing flame-retarded sheaths with non-flame-retarded insulations offers protection only below a critical external heat flux. Beyond this threshold, the sheath’s suppression capacity is exceeded, allowing the insulation to pyrolyze and significantly elevate the fire risk. While non-FR insulations are widely utilized for their dielectric strength, flexibility, durability, and cost-effectiveness, their contribution to fire growth remains a concern and requires further elucidation. Therefore, this study investigates the fire behavior of two industrial cables: MKEM-HF, comprising solely an FR sheath, and XMK-HF, consisting of an FR sheath over a highly flammable insulation, under a heat flux exceeding the sheath capacity to protect the inner insulation layer. Thermogravimetric (TGA) and Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) analyses were conducted to characterize thermal degradation of the cable layers and develop pyrolysis models. Cone calorimetry at 50 $$\rm kW \cdot m^{-2}$$ assessed fire behavior under gasification and flaming, for both single- and multi-cable configurations. MKEM-HF displayed a descending MLR-HRR profile over time, whereas XMK-HF exhibited a continuously rising trend with a dominant final peak, driven by the decomposition of the insulation. A classical 1D slab model of the cone calorimetry was used for inverse estimation of thermal properties and heats of combustion. A geometrical modification on the 1D model allowed the simulation of early insulation exposure, offering a possible approach for modeling the sheath’s mechanical rupture. A more advanced 2D model, accounting for cylindrical geometry and improved boundary coupling, demonstrated superior performance in transient heat transfer and peak prediction compared to the 1D model. The study highlights the critical influence of non-flame-retarded insulation on cable fire behavior and demonstrates the necessity of advanced modeling approaches beyond simple slab approximations to capture these effects.

papers.title: Meet the Two Organizations that Helped Create Fire Protection Engineering and Why it Still Matters Today
papers.abstract: For over 130 years, Underwriters Laboratories', 1 legacy has shaped daily life through groundbreaking research on new and emergency hazards, rigorous safety testing, and lifesaving standards.Now known as UL Research Institutes (ULRI), one of its most remarkable achievements remains largely unknown.In 1903, through a visionary partnership with the Armor Institute of Technology (today known as the Illinois Institute of Technology: Illinois Tech), Underwriters Laboratories established more than a new engineering degree program-they created the field of fire protection engineering as we know it.At ULRI, fire protection engineering remains as core to realizing its mission as it was in 1903. Born From TragedyThe timing was no accident.America was burning.The period between the 1860s and 1940s-dubbed by disaster historian Scott Gabriel Knowles as the "Conflagration Era" 2witnessed 18 of the 20 deadliest fires in American history.Urban conflagrations like the Great Chicago Fire (1871) and subsequent major fires in Boston (1872), Seattle (1889), Baltimore (1904), and the San Francisco earthquake and fire (1906) weren't just disasters; they were wake-up calls that traditional approaches to fire safety could fail catastrophically.The Conflagration Era overlapped the Progressive Era (1890s-1920s) -a time of great criticism and public mistrust in industrial and business practices and growing monopolies 1 In 2022 the organization known as Underwriters Laboratories became three independent safety science organizations: UL Research Institutes, UL Standards & Engagement, and UL Solutions.Each continue to share the mission of working for a safer world.In this article, Underwriters Laboratories is used throughout to refer to the historic organization prior to its transformation into three organizations in 2022.UL Research Institutes (or ULRI) is used throughout to refer to the contemporary organization which continues fire protection and prevention research among other areas of specialization.2 Knowles, Scott Gabriel.The Disaster Experts: Mastering Risk in Modern America.

papers.title: Advancing Automated Fire Safety Code Compliance: Automatic Annotation of BIM Door Elements
papers.abstract: Automated code compliance checking often faces challenges due to insufficient semantic information in Building Information Modeling (BIM) models, particularly during the early design stages, when only basic geometrical and alphanumerical information may be available. This study extends previous research on machine-learning-based annotation of ‘Exit’ doors by investigating whether additional BIM-derived features and adapted feature-engineering strategies can support the identification of both ‘Exit’ and ‘Apartment Exit’ doors in early-design residential architectural BIM models. A data-driven workflow was developed using features extracted from BIM models containing basic representations of doors, walls, stairs, and rooms, defined by their approximate geometry, dimensions, locations, and element types. For ‘Exit’ door classification, the model achieved an F1-score of 0.97 and produced correct predictions for the three test buildings used in the evaluation. For ‘Apartment Exit’ door classification, the integration of probability-encoded features improved the F1-score from 0.93 to 0.99 and increased the building-level test scores from [0.18, 0.47, 0.89, 1.00] to [0.82, 0.77, 0.95, 1.00] for the four test buildings, respectively. The results indicate that structured geometrical and alphanumerical information available in early-design BIM models can provide useful input for ML-based semantic enrichment of door elements. The main contributions of this study are: (1) the definition of eight BIM-derived spatial and topological features that can be extracted from basic building-element representations; (2) the adaptation of probability-encoded feature engineering to bounded integer-valued features using neighbor-based mean estimation for unseen values; and (3) the extension of the door-annotation workflow from ‘Exit’ to ‘Apartment Exit’ classification in Belgian high-rise buildings. The proposed approach is intended to support early-stage compliance checking by reducing the need for manual semantic annotation, while further validation on more diverse building datasets is required to assess broader generalizability.

papers.title: Study on the Fire Resistance and Scaling Laws of Geometrically Similar CFST Column Under Eccentric Compression
papers.abstract: Due to the high cost of full-scale fire tests, researchers often use scaled tests to evaluate the fire resistance of full-scale components. Traditional fire similarity theory requires proportional scaling of the heating curve. Small-scale models need higher heating rates, which are often beyond furnace limits, making scaled tests difficult in practice. To address this challenge, a thermo-mechanical sequential coupling method was developed and validated. A series of geometrically similar concrete-filled steel tubular (CFST) columns were designed. The study investigates the relationship between the fire resistance similarity ratio and the size ratio under the ISO-834 standard fire curve. The effects of eccentricity and load ratio on the fire resistance of geometrically similar CFST columns were also examined. The results show that: (i) The failure mode is independent of size. Axially loaded columns exhibit bulging failure, while in eccentrically loaded columns, the compression zone decreases and the tension zone expands as eccentricity increases; (ii) The fire resistance decreases significantly with increasing eccentricity and load ratio, with stronger effects observed in larger columns; (iii) At small eccentricity or load ratio, the fire resistance is governed by the interaction between the concrete core and steel tube, whereas at large eccentricity or load ratio, it is mainly determined by the steel tube; (iv) An empirical formula considering eccentricity and load ratio is proposed, providing guidance for scaled fire tests of CFST columns.

papers.title: Improvement Forecasts for Asynchronous Observations in Data-Driven Wildfire Spread Prediction
papers.abstract: Data assimilation (DA) methods enhance the accuracy of prediction models by integrating observational data. Due to the large scale of wildfires, the observed fire perimeter may consist of fire front segments from multiple time points, which are referred to as asynchronous observations. Asynchronous observations contain lag errors that are not accounted for by traditional DA algorithms. This paper proposes an Ensemble Transform Kalman filter incorporating a centralized extrapolation strategy (ETKF-centralized) to reduce the lag error associated with asynchronous fire fronts. To evaluate the performance of ETKF-centralized, a landscape wildfire is simulated using PROMETHEUS to generate asynchronous observations. Since the actual mechanism of wildfire spread cannot be fully captured during prediction, we selected a different model, FARSITE, as a basic prediction model. The results show that the similarity index of ETKF-centralized forecast fire exceeds 0.85 with a lead time of 4 h, and the root mean square error is reduced by 29% compared with standard ETKF. Furthermore, ETKF-centralized is successfully applied to a 900 m2 field experiment, demonstrating its strong potential for application in wildfire forecasting.

papers.title: Using Multimodal Large Language Models for False Alarm Reduction in Image-Based Fire Detection
papers.abstract: Existing vision-based methods suffer from high false alarm rates in urban flame detection. Applying Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) for secondary filtering shows great potential for reducing false alarms, yet they have high inference latency and are prone to reasoning collapse on negative samples without explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) guidance. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes Flash-Cascade, the first sub-second MLLM-based firewall that leverages CoT for efficiently filtering false alarms. We deconstructed the flame detection process into four logical stages (planning, observation, analysis, and judgment), which informed the design of three switchable reasoning modes (Detailed, Quick, and Rapid) to achieve inference acceleration via CoT compression. We fine-tuned Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct on a multi-granularity instruction dataset via Low-Rank Adaptation. This process decoupled the model’s discriminative capability from long-form text generation, thereby enabling robust performance even without explicit CoT guidance. On our newly constructed benchmark incorporating real-world hard negatives, Flash-Cascade achieves an accuracy of 97.79% and an F1-score of 0.977 in Rapid mode, outperforming the zero-shot baseline by 61.63 percentage points (pp) and 0.515, respectively. Furthermore, it outperforms the state-of-the-art object detector DEIMv2 by 14.64 pp in accuracy. The method exhibits exceptional sample efficiency, converging with only 600 samples and 2 epochs, and improves inference speed by 810% over standard CoT. This study opens new avenues for robust and efficient flame detection in high-interference scenarios.

papers.title: Parametric Analysis and Predictive Modeling for Post-fire Ventilation Following CO2 Fire Extinguishment
papers.abstract: Low-pressure carbon dioxide fire suppression systems, while effectively extinguishing fires in enclosed spaces, create a high-concentration CO2 environment that poses a significant safety risk to personnel. Designing an efficient post-fire ventilation system to reduce the CO2 volume fraction to a safe level is therefore of critical importance. This study integrates full-scale fire suppression experiments with PyroSim numerical simulations to investigate the post-fire ventilation process following CO2 extinguishment. A CFD model was developed, calibrated (turbulent Schmidt number Sct = 0.7), and validated against three experimental cases (mean R2 = 0.97, RMSE = 0.62). Parametric analysis revealed that the air change rate (ACH) is the dominant parameter governing ventilation efficiency, with 12 h− 1 recommended as the optimal value. The airflow organization — specifically, a centralized top-supply, bottom-exhaust configuration with vents on the same side — significantly influences the dilution rate by working synergistically with the natural buoyancy-driven stratification of CO2. Based on the optimized configuration, 27 simulation scenarios spanning nine initial CO2 volume fractions (14%-54%) and three ACH values (8, 12, 20 h− 1) were simulated. A predictive model for the safety ventilation duration was derived through log-linear regression (R2 = 0.99), providing a quantitative tool for post-fire ventilation system design and risk assessment.

papers.title: Study on Axial Bearing Performance of Reactive Powder Concrete-Filled Square Steel Tube Columns After High Temperature
papers.abstract: This study investigated the axial compressive behavior of reactive powder concrete-filled steel tube (RPC-FST) columns after high temperatures. To evaluate the effects of heating duration, spiral stirrup spacing, and steel tube thickness on the post-fire performance of RPC-FST columns, ten specimens were first subjected to high-temperature tests and then subjected to axial compression load tests. The experimental results indicate that all specimens exhibited local buckling failure. The severity of local buckling decreased with increasing steel tube thickness and heating duration, as well as with decreasing spiral stirrup spacing. Compared with the unheated specimens, the specimens with heating times ranging from 140 to 260 min showed a reduction of 2.18–37.46% in the ultimate load and 11.00–38.51% in the elastic stiffness. Under identical heating conditions, the ultimate load increased with increasing steel tube thickness and decreasing spiral stirrup spacing. Specifically, when the steel tube thickness increased from 4 to 10 mm, the ultimate load capacity and elastic stiffness increased by 21.98 and 19.35%, respectively. Moreover, reducing the spiral stirrup spacing from 80 to 40 mm resulted in a 23.30% increase in ultimate load capacity. Based on the experimental results, a calculation method for predicting the axial bearing capacity of RPC-FST columns after high temperature was proposed. The proposed method was evaluated against the experimental results, existing design specifications, and previously reported prediction models, demonstrating its applicability and providing useful references for future research.
