papers.title: Effect of Fabric Stretch on the Thermal Protective Performance of Firefighter Clothing: An Experimental and 3D Numerical Analysis
papers.abstract: During firefighting operations, movements such as bending elbows and knees induce deformation of the outer shell material, affecting the thermal protective performance (TPP) of firefighter clothing. However, the effects of fabric stretching under different thermal environments and the associated microstructural mechanisms remain unclear. To investigate this, experiments were conducted at four stretch levels (0%, 3%, 6%, 12%) under three thermal conditions (8.5 kW/m2 radiant heat, 30 kW/m2 flame, 84 kW/m2 hybrid heat), measuring fabric structural properties and TPP. Results indicated that stretching reduced fabric porosity and slightly increased thickness, with TPP decreasing more noticeably under low-radiation heat. To elucidate the heat transfer mechanisms, a three-dimensional finite element model incorporating yarn geometry and air pores was developed. Simulations revealed that stretch-induced structural changes enhanced the intrinsic thermal insulation performance (TIP) of the fabric. Parametric analyses further showed that increasing surface convection produced only minor changes in thermal resistance, whereas increasing fiber thermal conductivity resulted in a more noticeable reduction. Combined experimental and simulation results demonstrated that changes in TPP were governed by the competing effects of (i) improved thermal insulation due to increased fabric thickness and (ii) enhanced conductive heat transfer due to increased fiber–sensor contact area. Although stretching increased TIP, the latter effect dominated, resulting in lower TPP values. These findings elucidate the heat transfer mechanisms of stretched fabrics and support TPP evaluation considering fabric deformation. They also provide practical guidance for the design of firefighting suits with adequate ease allowances in body regions undergoing substantial movement, thereby improving firefighter thermal protection and safety.

papers.title: Analysis of Temperature Distribution in Steel-Concrete Composite Beams with Concrete Hollow Core Slabs with Rectangular Openings Under Fire Conditions
papers.abstract: The structural contribution of slab in steel–concrete composite beams depends on the interaction between materials. Despite providing procedures for temperature evolution and strength reduction in composite beams with solid slabs, NBR 14,323 does not include specific recommendations for systems that incorporate hollow-core slabs. Towards addressing that knowledge gap, this manuscript reports on a comprehensive parametric numerical investigation of temperature distribution in steel–concrete composite beams that incorporate hollow-core concrete slabs with rectangular openings. Building upon previous research, the study evaluates rectangular openings, expands the range of concrete densities to six classes (1,750-3,000 kg/m³), and increases the numerical database from 60 to 120 thermal models. The expanded database enables a systematic assessment of the combined influence of opening geometry and concrete density on the thermal response of hollow-core slabs and provides new temperature distribution tables suitable for future code development. According to the results, six tables show the temperature variation along the slab depth for densities ranging from 1,750 to 3,000 kg/m³, indicating hollow-core slabs consistently develop higher temperatures than those prescribed by NBR 14,323 for solid slabs of same density. The results also show opening geometry substantially affects the temperature distribution, with differences of up to 85.8 °C between rectangular and circular openings in function of slab layer and fire exposure time. Therefore, both internal geometry and concrete density should be considered for the development of future structural fire design provisions for hollow-core slab systems. The aforementioned tables provide a preliminary technical basis for assessments of the thermal behavior of hollow-core slabs with rectangular openings and may support future improvements to structural fire design provisions for steel–concrete composite beams.

papers.title: Synergistic Suppression of Coal Dust Explosions by a Novel Phosphorus-Grafted Fly Ash Composite: Preparation, Performance, and Mechanism
papers.abstract: Coal dust explosions pose a severe threat to industrial safety, while the large-scale disposal of fly ash (FA) presents a significant environmental challenge. To utilize this industrial solid waste for safety applications, a novel phosphorus-modified fly ash composite explosion suppressant (FA@H3PO4) was developed. The suppressant was synthesized via alkali activation pretreatment followed by phosphoric acid grafting. Characterization using SEM, EDS, and FTIR confirmed that the modification effectively increased the surface roughness of FA and successfully introduced phosphorus-containing flame-retardant groups. Explosion suppression performance was evaluated in a visual vertical combustion tube, where FA@H3PO4 demonstrated significantly superior performance compared to raw FA. At a concentration of 60 wt%, the modified agent reduced the flame propagation velocity to 2.6 m/s, resulting in a discontinuous “ghost flame” structure; the peak flame temperature was drastically suppressed to approximately 241 °C, compared to 1285 °C for pure coal dust. Furthermore, the addition of 60 wt% FA@H3PO4 led to an 80% decrease in maximum explosion pressure (Pmax) and a 100% extension of the time to peak pressure. Thermal analysis (TG) reveals that the suppression mechanism relies on a synergistic effect: the physical cooling and barrier function of the fly ash skeleton, combined with the chemical scavenging of free radicals by the grafted phosphorus groups. This study provides a cost-effective and efficient technical pathway for coal dust explosion control.

papers.title: Real-Time Visibility Enhancement in Fire Scenes Using Edge-Guided Physical Smoke Removal
papers.abstract: The degradation of visibility caused by fire and smoke severely hinders surveillance, leading to delayed decision-making and rescue operations during disasters. Existing smoke and haze removal approaches often struggle with dynamic lighting, heavy smoke, and real-time processing requirements, as they either rely on physical models or deep learning (DL) methods. The enhanced images thus suffer from loss of edge details and over-enhancement in some cases. To address these difficulties, a novel Dark Channel Edge Enhancement Pipeline with CLAHE Fusion (DEEP-CF), a hybrid framework that integrates physics-based and edge-preserving enhancement methods through a multi-stage fusion, is proposed. DEEP-CF uses luminance-based dark channel estimation, edge-aware guided filtering, adaptive rescaling, and dual-stage fusion with CLAHE to enhance both contrast and structure. The implementation ensures real-time performance by leveraging GPUs and achieves up to 44 FPS on 640x480 resolution video streams. Qualitative and quantitative evaluation on the ’Indoor Fire Smoke Dataset’ and real-world scenes demonstrate competitive perceptual quality, smoke intensity reduction, and structural and edge detail preservation compared to other traditional models and improved downstream object detection performance. The results on the evaluation metrics of BIQME, BRISQUE, NIQE, CFI, PSNR, SSIM, EPI, and VIF establish the proposed DEEP-CF pipeline as a favorable perceptual quality enhancer and a computationally efficient, balanced solution for visibility enhancement in dynamic fire and smoke scenes.

papers.title: Numerical Study on Fire Resistance of Square UHPC Filled Steel Tubular Slender Columns Under Axial Compression
papers.abstract: The mechanical response mechanisms of square ultra high performance concrete filled steel tubular (UHPCFST) columns under elevated temperatures differ significantly from those of conventional concrete filled steel tubular (CFST) columns; however, related investigations remain scarce. In this study, a validated thermo-mechanically coupled finite element model was developed to systematically evaluate the effects of section size, slenderness ratio, steel ratio, and load level on the fire resistance of square UHPCFST columns, and to elucidate the distinct load-bearing mechanisms of UHPCFST and CFST columns under fire conditions. The results demonstrate that section size, slenderness ratio, steel ratio, and load level significantly affect fire resistance. Specifically, increasing the section size from 200 to 1000 mm improves fire resistance by approximately 123.5%, whereas increasing the slenderness ratio from 30 to 70 decreases it by 57.4%. Conversely, the effect of material strength is relatively insignificant. At the same load level, UHPCFST columns exhibit 15%–45% lower fire resistance than CFST columns, but demonstrate enhanced load-sharing efficiency between the steel tube and core concrete. Based on the parametric study, a calculation method for predicting the fire resistance of rectangular UHPCFST columns is proposed.

papers.title: Evaluation of Porosity and Pore Diameter of Gypsum Boards at Elevated Temperatures
papers.abstract: Gypsum boards are widely used as passive fire protection materials due to their ability to delay heat transfer through endothermic dehydration of calcium sulfate dihydrate (CaSO 4 ·2 H 2 O). Understanding the temperature-dependent evolution of porosity and pore size distributions in gypsum board is essential for defining microstructural parameters used in fire-scale thermal transport models. In particular, the evolution of pore structure during dehydration and high-temperature degradation influences heat transfer within the material and therefore affects its fire protection capability. Quantitative data describing how the pore structure evolves at high temperatures remain scarce, limiting the accuracy of multi-physics fire simulations. This work experimentally characterizes the temperature-dependent evolution of porosity and pore size distributions in gypsum board exposed to temperatures up to 1000°C. Samples subjected to controlled thermal treatments were analyzed using mercury intrusion porosimetry, optical microscopy, and large-area optical scanning in order to capture pore structures across multiple length scales. The resulting dataset provides a comprehensive description of pore structure evolution associated with dehydration, fragmentation, and high-temperature sintering processes. The experiments reveal a bimodal pore system consisting of micro-pores (< 10 μm) formed during dehydration and stable meso-/macro-pores (10–100 μm) generated by foaming agents. Total porosity increases with temperature, while the average pore diameter decreases, indicating pore multiplication rather than coalescence. The experimentally measured pore characteristics were incorporated into a microstructure-informed thermal transport model (GPRO: Gypsum PROperties) in order to evaluate the influence of representative pore length scales on the radiative component of heat transfer and to assess their impact on the effective thermal conductivity (k eff ). Model predictions were compared with literature data for the effective thermal conductivity of gypsum board at elevated temperatures to assess the consistency of the derived microstructural parameters with independently measured macroscopic properties. The results show that the evolution of total porosity strongly affects the conductive component of heat transfer, while the radiative conductivity predicted by diffusion-based radiation models is primarily controlled by pore lengths in the meso-scale range identified in the experimental measurements. Sensitivity analysis indicates that variations in representative pore diameter between 1 μm and 100 μm lead to changes in predicted effective thermal conductivity below 3%. Within diffusion-based radiative heat-transfer formulations, this behaviour reflects the dominance of meso-scale pore lengths in the radiative contribution. The temperature-resolved microstructural dataset presented in this work provides experimentally grounded parameters for thermal modelling of gypsum-based fire protection materials and contributes to improved representation of porous insulation behaviour in fire safety engineering simulations. The resulting temperature-resolved microstructural dataset, linking dehydration, microstructural evolution and temperature-dependent porosity, delivers experimentally grounded parameters for thermal modelling of gypsum-based fire protection materials and contributes to improved representation of porous insulation behavior in fire safety engineering simulations.

papers.title: The Relevance of Law and Economics for Fire Safety
papers.abstract: This article investigates how the discipline of Law and Economics (“L&E”) can guide legal frameworks for fire safety by aligning legal rules, economic incentives, and engineering practices. We first introduce core L&E concepts – externalities, information asymmetries, public-goods, and liability structures – and their relevance for fire safety. We then develop a mathematical model for the total cost of fire (for a design problem or building portfolio), and use this model to contrast prescriptive and performance-based regimes and compare three liability standards (strict liability, code-compliance negligence, and due-diligence negligence). When considering a full internalization of the cost of fire (i.e., when the private decision-maker carries all fire-related costs), our analyses show that prescriptive regimes generate over- or under-investment in preventive measures, resulting in sub-optimal societal outcomes. Performance-based regimes, on the other hand, provide private decision makers with the incentive to invest up to societally optimal safety investments. The comparison of liability regimes shows that the internalization of the cost of fire is most effectively achieved by the strict liability regime. A liability regime of negligence based on due diligence (professional standards) also pushes private decision-makers towards adopting societally optimum designs. However, when negligence is established by the (lack of) compliance with prescriptive fire safety codes, this results in societally suboptimal designs. These results imply that policymakers should favor adaptable, efficiency-oriented regulatory designs, and highlight that liability regimes should be calibrated to internalize fire safety related costs. In more general terms, the results demonstrate the power of L&E approaches for supporting discussions on fire safety legislation.

papers.title: Evaluating the Cost-Effectiveness of Interlinked Fire Alarm Systems in Scotland and England
papers.abstract: This paper applies the J value framework to assess when interlinked domestic fire alarm systems would be cost effective in Scotland and England. Pre policy national statistics pool dwellings with no alarms, standalone alarms (the vast majority), and some interlinked systems, so they do not identify the marginal effect of interlinking. We therefore present threshold (break-even) conditions: combinations of reductions in fatalities, injuries, and direct property damage that yield J ≤ 1 for self and professional installation, using historical statistics only as non-causal, illustrative anchors for sensitivity analyses. It was found that, across both countries, damage reduction is the dominant driver of cost-effectiveness, followed by fatality reduction; injury reduction has limited influence (assuming direct injury costs only). One-way thresholds indicate that achieving $$\:J\le\:1$$ typically requires around 30–60% reduction in direct property damage, with fatality thresholds generally around 40–80% depending on installation method and region. Two-factor (damage and fatality) thresholds show trade-offs between these reductions, with more demanding conditions in England due to higher expected damage per fire. Tornado analyses centred on an illustrative base case confirm that installation cost and damage-related inputs exert the greatest influence on $$\:J$$ , while societal discount rates have modest effects. Interlinked systems can be cost effective where installed costs are lower (for example self-installation) and reductions in property damage, and secondarily fatalities, are moderate to large. Improved data on alarm type and performance, property-damage costs, and near-misses would enable movement from threshold analysis to causal evaluation.

papers.title: Analysis of Thermohydraulic Spalling in Blended Cement Concrete
papers.abstract: Recently, the construction industry has increasingly focused on the development of more sustainable transport infrastructure, such as tunnels, driven by the growing use of clinker-reduced cements. One major challenge in this context is fire exposure, which can lead to severe structural damage through concrete spalling, thereby compromising the integrity of the structure. To date, the fire-induced spalling behavior of blended cement concrete remains insufficiently understood. This is particularly concerning, given the increasing adoption of blended cements with reduced clinker content, which are expected to see widespread use in the future. Consequently, a deeper understanding of how different cement types influence spalling susceptibility is of great importance. A comprehensive study was conducted to investigate spalling behavior and analyze the associated thermohydraulic effects in concretes made with CEM I, CEM II/A-LL, CEM III/A, and CEM II/B-Q. The findings revealed that the use of blended cements generally led to increased spalling susceptibility, even in normal-strength concrete. Additional analysis indicated that blended cement concretes exhibited lower permeability and higher moisture content, both of which are likely contributors to the elevated spalling risk. Furthermore, the study showed that moisture transport during heating closely follows the dehydration behavior of the cementitious matrix. Blended cement pastes were found to contain lower quantities of early-dehydrating AFt and AFm phases, as well as more thermally stable C-(A)-S-H phases. Moreover, the incorporation of polypropylene fibers into the concrete mix effectively mitigated spalling across all cement types. Therefore, demonstrating the continued effectiveness of polypropylene fibers as a spalling prevention strategy.

papers.title: Battery Abuse Testing and Thermal Runaway Propagation
papers.abstract: Thermal runaway (TR) propagation is an essential characteristic of larger lithium-ion battery fires. Cell- and module-level battery abuse tests have been conducted using large-format NMC pouch cells. In both test campaigns, heating was used to trigger TR. An electrical heater was used for the cell-level tests, and heat exposure to an external flame was used to trigger a cell-to-cell propagating TR in the modules. Cell surface temperatures were measured during both test campaigns to evaluate thermal runaway properties, including TR onset temperatures, TR max temperatures, and TR heating rates, as a function of local heating rates. The TR propagation characteristics in the modules were analysed based on the module’s temperature distribution and heat release rate. A comparison between the conditions during single-cell and full-module tests was conducted to evaluate their effects on TR and, ultimately, to determine whether cell tests are representative of the conditions during a passive propagation test or a real Lithium-ion battery fire scenario.

papers.title: Fire Dynamics and Surface Oxygen Measurement During Vertical, Buoyancy-Driven Turbulent Fire Spread
papers.abstract: Oxygen availability at a pyrolyzing surface during turbulent flame spread remains poorly understood, and the governing fire dynamics are not yet fundamentally resolved. A series of experiments was conducted using a wall-corner configuration to measure surface oxygen concentrations during flame spread at two distinct locations under a $${300}\,\textrm{kW}$$ hood, using both burner-generated and solid-fuel-generated flame conditions. In burner tests, a propane burner was positioned at the base corner, with mass flow adjusted to achieve steady HRRs. In solid-fuel tests (PMMA, Douglas Fir), ignition was initiated at a $${30}\,\textrm{kW}$$ propane HRR. Gas sampling tubes were flush-mounted to one of the panels at a vertical height of $${100}\,\textrm{cm}$$ above the burner and at lateral distances of $${10}\,\textrm{cm}$$ and $${20}\,\textrm{cm}$$ from the corner to extract combustion gases. A novel technique was introduced to non-intrusively estimate surface oxygen availability using a correlation between the measured oxygen volume fraction and the normalized image intensities. Radiation intensity measurements were used to quantify fire growth rates, which were, on average, 3.5 times greater in the vertical direction than in the horizontal. Flame sheet growth and acceleration were found to directly influence the measured surface oxygen volume fractions. Time-resolved surface oxygen fields were reconstructed for PMMA, providing new insight into oxygen depletion dynamics across distinct pyrolysis regimes during a turbulent fire spread.

papers.title: Developing Empirical and Graphical Indices for Fire-Induced Spalling of Concrete
papers.abstract: Fire-induced spalling remains an ongoing concern for concrete structures exposed to fire conditions as existing predictive methods struggle to achieve reliable predictions. To bridge this knowledge gap, this study proposes a methodology to develop empirically driven indices to predict the spalling phenomenon. The methodology comprises three approaches: systematic data transformations, logistic regression, and a data-informed boundary decision based on machine learning (ML). The obtained indices, evaluated over a comprehensive dataset of over 1,000 fire tests and 200,000 cases, exhibited an accuracy ranging from 71–82%. The proposed indices were then refined per concrete grade and achieved improved performance. These findings highlight the potential for developing empirical indices to arrive at simple and easy to use tools to predict fire-induced spalling of concrete. Such indices could set the stage for new predictive methods that go beyond simple statistical and ML inference approaches in the near future.

papers.title: The Hidden Variable: How Data Gaps Shape Battery Fire Safety Engineering
papers.abstract: Lithium-ion battery systems are increasingly deployed across vehicles, buildings, and energy infrastructure, raising urgent fire safety challenges that are not yet fully addressed by existing codes and standards. This article presents findings from an international survey of fire safety professionals with experience in battery-related projects, designed to capture current practice, perceived gaps, and methodological limitations. The survey reveals strong reliance on heat release rate as a principal design parameter, yet limited recognition of the uncertainties associated with its measurement. Respondents emphasized the lack of validated, system-level test data, particularly on gas composition (primarily toxicity but also flammability), and concerns related to UL9540A goals, quality and interpretation. Concerns about transparency and unequal access to test data were repeatedly noted, alongside the absence of harmonized regulatory guidance across regions. Taken together, the results provide one of the first systematic insights into how fire safety engineers approach battery fire safety design/strategy in projects involving battery systems in practice and identify areas where research, regulation, and industry practice must converge to enable safe large-scale deployment of battery systems.

papers.title: Finding and Understanding the Limiting Oxygen Concentration for Oxygen Reduction Systems
papers.abstract: Automated storage systems and large-scale freezers can be challenging for conventional fire protection systems. Instead, an oxygen reduction system (ORS) could be a suitable option. In an ORS the design oxygen concentration is the key parameter for the level of protection achieved by the system. However, current methods for determining this concentration yield varying results and either require large and complex test setups or arrive at overly optimistic levels for protection. In this paper, an experimental method for using the controlled atmosphere cone calorimeter (CACC) to find the limiting oxygen concentration at extinction (LOC ext ) is proposed. The results from the CACC showed good agreement with limiting oxygen concentrations (LOC) determined by large-scale; indicating that the CACC could serve as a cost-effective alternative for determining the LOC of ordinary combustibles for ORS applications. Furthermore, thermal analysis and experiments using both nitrogen and carbon dioxide highlights that the thermal properties of the diluent gas, rather than oxygen displacement and chemical quenching, are the primary factors influencing the LOC. Hence, the findings in this paper increase the understanding of ORS systems and offer a way to determine the LOC for ORS based on small-scale testing.

papers.title: A Hybrid FEM-Surrogate Enhanced Framework for Thermo-Mechanical Degradation in Concrete Beams Under Hydrocarbon Fire
papers.abstract: Concrete structures exposed to elevated temperatures undergo progressive thermal and mechanical degradation, compromising serviceability and safety. This study examines plain cement concrete (PCC) and reinforced cement concrete (RCC) beams across multiple grades subjected to hydrocarbon fire, integrating finite element modelling (FEM) with calibrated surrogate models. A curated dataset spanning temperature, grade, and beam type supports the training of Gaussian process regression (GPR), support vector regression (SVR), and gradient boosted machines (GBM). Cross validation with standardized residuals provides diagnostic calibration, while external benchmarking against independent FEM simulations ensures physical consistency. Results indicate that the effective thermal conductivity indicator $$k_{\textrm{eff}}$$ , derived from transient thermal field outputs under Eurocode-consistent temperature-dependent conductivity inputs, decreases with temperature in a manner consistent with moisture loss and microstructural evolution in heated concrete, while thermo-mechanical response reveals sharp escalation of displacements beyond $$500^{\circ }\textrm{C}$$ , rapid crack width expansion after $$350^{\circ }\textrm{C}$$ , and concentration of von Mises stresses at beam edges. Across most targets and materials, GPR achieves the strongest overall fidelity and provides calibrated predictive dispersion, while GBM yields the lowest PCC crack-width error and SVR exhibits the largest deviations in strongly nonlinear regimes. Design charts and three-dimensional response surfaces, overlaid with FEM samples, provide practitioner tools for risk-aware screening. The integrated FEM-surrogate framework offers computational efficiency while preserving accuracy, enabling rapid assessment of fire-induced behaviour and aligning with performance-based design strategies for resilient infrastructure.

papers.title: Reaction to Fire of Birch Plywood Bonded with Three Different Adhesive Systems at Multiple Scales
papers.abstract: This study investigates the reaction to fire of 9-layer birch plywood bonded with three industrially relevant adhesive systems: urea formaldehyde (UF), melamine urea formaldehyde (MUF), and phenol formaldehyde (PF). Panels were prepared under standardized conditions and evaluated at multiple scales—ranging from fuel property characterisation and thermogravimetric analysis to bench-scale cone calorimetry and ignition testing in the single flame test (SFT). A self-constructed Mini-SBI test (downscaled single burning item test) was developed to capture intermediate-scale reaction to fire with a focus on the orientation of the surface veneer layer. Results reveal that UF-bonded plywood, particularly with lengthwise-oriented surface veneers, exhibited the most critical fire response, including increased susceptibility to ignition during extended localized flame exposure and fire growth promoted by adhesive-controlled veneer separation. PF-bonded samples showed greater thermal stability and higher char formation. MUF-bonded samples exhibited comparatively favourable ignition behaviour, while smoke-production differences among the adhesive systems were not statistically significant. Differences in thermal degradation and flammability highlight the influence of adhesive chemistry and veneer orientation on the reaction to fire of the material. The Mini-SBI setup differentiated between material variants and demonstrated its potential as a material-efficient intermediate-scale method for comparative fire testing during product development. This work highlights the need for adhesive-specific consideration in fire safety assessments of engineered wood products.

papers.title: Estimation of Excess Inhalation Non‐Cancer and Cancer Risk From Volatile Organic Compound Mixtures in New York City Nail Salons
papers.abstract: Nail salon workers are acutely and chronically exposed to mixtures of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), yet health risks in New York City (NYC) salons have not been systematically assessed. We performed an occupational risk assessment using integrated real‐time total VOC (TVOC) monitoring and chemical‐specific sampling of 11 VOCs across five NYC salons. Median and peak exposures and their 95th percentile (upper‐bound) values were used in non‐cancer and cancer risk models using deterministic and probabilistic approaches. Deterministic non‐cancer risk modeling indicated hazard indices (HIs) were generally below the benchmark value of 1, with exceedances observed only using upper‐bound exposures in the salon with the highest VOC concentrations. The probabilistic non‐cancer assessment showed a similar pattern, with some salons having non‐negligible probabilities of HI exceedance despite median HIs below 1. Deterministic and probabilistic benzene cancer risk assessments indicated exceedances of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) de minimis benchmark under multiple exposure scenarios. Although VOC concentrations were below occupational exposure limits (OELs), incorporating exposure variability and uncertainty identified elevated non‐cancer and cancer risks under certain scenarios. Previous research has linked nail salon work to adverse health effects, including respiratory symptoms and developmental and reproductive effects, suggesting that current OELs may not adequately protect this workforce. Our results highlight the need for improved exposure limits, chemical mixture risk assessment methods, and health protections for nail salon workers.

papers.title: Virtual Flood Experience Enhances Preparedness Through Emotional and Neural Engagement
papers.abstract: As climate change intensifies flood risks, strengthening individual preparedness is essential for sustainable societies. This study tested whether first‐person three‐dimensional computer graphics (3DCG) flood videos can complement official flood maps in motivating preparedness. We used these materials as operationalizations of experiential and descriptive information, respectively. In a preregistered web experiment with 1000 participants, those who viewed flood videos showed a small but statistically significant increase in preparedness intentions compared with those who viewed flood maps. Mediation analyses showed that, among the measured psychological variables, only fear had a significant indirect effect, suggesting that stimulus‐evoked fear helped explain this increase. We also conducted a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) study with 45 participants using a within‐subjects design. Flood videos elicited greater right amygdala activation than flood maps, consistent with fear‐related processing. Together, these findings provide convergent behavioral and neural evidence that first‐person 3DCG flood videos evoke stronger fear‐related responses than flood maps and that subjective fear helps account for their effect on preparedness intentions. The results suggest that visually vivid flood videos may complement map‐based communication by increasing emotional salience and promoting flood‐preparedness intentions.

papers.title: Hybrid Semi‐Quantitative Risk Assessment for Aging Offshore Platforms: A HAZOP–FMEA–Bow‐Tie Framework With Sensitivity Analysis and KRI‐Based Governance
papers.abstract: Aging offshore installations increasingly operate beyond their original design life, yet conventional periodic risk assessments capture barrier degradation only intermittently. This study presents a barrier‐conditioned semi‐quantitative risk‐assessment workflow that integrates Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), and bow‐tie barrier analysis. The workflow combines decomposed residual likelihood and consequence scoring with threshold‐stability testing and a Key Risk Indicator (KRI)‐based update rule. Its principal contribution is the governance linkage: an explicit rule set that maps barrier condition and KRI threshold breaches to changes in residual likelihood, residual consequence, and risk band between formal safety‐case reviews. To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the workflow is demonstrated through a fully synthetic scenario representing a life‐extended semi‐submersible installation; all inputs are constructed and explicitly identified throughout as scenario assumptions. Under the illustrative scoring assumptions, a 19‐hazard register spanning seven hazard categories yields two high, nine medium, and eight low residual risks, with blowout/well‐control failure and hydrogen sulfide release remaining the highest residual risks. Per‐perturbation threshold‐stability analysis and distribution‐based Monte Carlo propagation indicate that 16 of the 19 residual risk ratings are sensitive to classification boundaries, suggesting that the reported scores should be interpreted as central estimates subject to uncertainty. The proposed workflow provides a transparent tool for risk screening and governance support, complementing full quantitative risk assessment (QRA) while preserving its essential analytical role.

papers.title: Identification and Governance Strategy of Urban Systemic Risk Induced by Extreme Rain–Snow–Ice Weather in Southern China
papers.abstract: China's rapid urbanization has expanded urban spatial scale and increased the concentration of population, wealth, and infrastructure. Against the background of climate change, urban systemic risk induced by extreme rain–snow–ice weather (USR–RSI) in southern China has repeatedly disrupted critical infrastructure and public services, generating cascading impacts across interconnected urban systems. This study examines the generation and evolution of USR–RSI and develops a corresponding resilience governance strategy. Building on conceptual analysis, complex network theory and system vulnerability theory are integrated to construct the theoretical framework. A causal loop diagram is used to characterize risk diffusion and feedback mechanisms based on the 2008 and 2024 RSI disaster cases. Semi‐structured interviews and documentary materials are further analyzed using a structured data analysis approach to identify sensitivity and adaptive factors associated with node and path vulnerability. On the basis of these findings, a whole‐process resilience governance framework is proposed, covering resilience construction, integration of warning and response, rapid recovery, and long‐term adaptive optimization and transformative reconfiguration. The study provides an empirical and analytical basis for understanding and governing USR–RSI from the perspective of interconnected urban socio‐technical systems.

papers.title: The Aftermath of Almost: Communicating Risk Amid Community Narratives of Near Misses
papers.abstract: Unpredictable weather means that serious threats do not always unfold as forecast. Hurricane near misses create an especially challenging communication context: The absence of harm may invite community explanations that make the event feel less threatening, even as future risk persists. This study examines how community narratives and post‐event risk messages shape risk perception, collective efficacy, preparedness intentions, message sharing, and credibility after hurricane near misses. In an online experiment, Florida residents ( N = 405) viewed social media posts about a hurricane that shifted away from a coastal community. The posts varied by explanation type, comparing a symbolic community narrative with a factual account, and by response source, comparing emergency management, peer, and control messages. Results show limits and leverage points for post‐event risk communication: In the primary analysis, neither community narratives nor risk messages significantly shifted perceived risk; however, supplementary analyses accounting for regional residence revealed a small reduction in perceived risk following narrative exposure. Risk messages increased sharing and collective efficacy, and organizational sources were more credible than peer sources. These findings suggest that post‐event risk communication after near misses may not readily recalibrate individual risk perceptions but can shape how risk information circulates and how communities perceive their capacity to respond. The study advances understanding of near misses as ambiguous risk events in which communication matters even when harm does not occur.

papers.title: Risk‐Oriented Differentiated Governance for Ambiguous Information
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence has led to an exponential increase in false information, especially ambiguous information. Hampered by resource constraints, conventional governance approaches fall short of enabling efficient and precise risk management. In response, this paper innovatively proposes a risk‐oriented tiered governance framework tailored to ambiguous information. Specifically, we quantify epistemic uncertainty via multi‐level semantic features, combine it with network propagation features to determine latent influence scores, and construct a risk function capturing their synergy. Critical and acceptable boundaries are introduced to categorize ambiguous information into discrete risk levels, tier‐specific governance strategies are devised, and a propagation throttling (limiting each user's successful forwards per ambiguous information) strategy is innovatively proposed for medium‐risk information. Finally, we simulate differentiated governance strategies across risk levels of ambiguous information, systematically assess governance effectiveness, and offer a comparative discussion grounded in fairness and ethics. This study offers an operational analytical framework for refined risk governance of ambiguous information, contributes methodological innovations in risk quantification modeling and tiered governance strategies, and provides theoretical support and practical guidance for risk management authorities in designing differentiated measures.

papers.title: Explainable Machine Learning for Risk‐Driven Forecasting of Global Food Commodity Prices: Geopolitical, Logistic, and Energy Drivers
papers.abstract: Escalating geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, and energy market volatility have intensified global food price instability, posing serious risks to food security. To address this challenge, this study proposes an explainable forecasting framework that integrates historical price dynamics with external drivers, applied to five essential food commodities, olive oil, eggs, chicken, beef, and bread, over the period 1990–2023. The analysis examines how logistics efficiency, energy costs, and geopolitical uncertainty relate to food prices through complex, nonlinear relationships. Going beyond conventional models, the proposed nonlinear autoregressive neural network with exogenous inputs (NARX) captures these dynamics while preserving explainability: through an ablation‐style comparison against a baseline autoregressive model, it systematically evaluates alternative panels of exogenous inputs to identify those with the greatest forecasting contribution. The results show that the predictive relevance of exogenous panels varies across commodities and evaluation metrics, and underscore the value of transparent, multidimensional analysis for improving food price forecasting and understanding price dynamics in an increasingly uncertain global context.

papers.title: Assessing the Relative Contribution of Pre‐Deployment Abroad Versus In‐Mission Dirofilaria immitis Infections in French Military Working Dogs Screened Post‐Mission: A Quantitative Risk Assessment
papers.abstract: Dirofilaria immitis ( D. immitis ) is a mosquito‐borne nematode responsible for canine cardiopulmonary dirofilariasis, a parasitic infection widely distributed worldwide and established in mainland France, particularly in southern regions. Military working dogs (MWDs) may be at increased risk of exposure to vector‐borne pathogens because of their predominantly outdoor lifestyle and frequent missions abroad. Nevertheless, D. immitis infection remains sporadic in this population, likely due to well‐implemented medical prophylaxis. The aim of this study was to investigate the likely origin of D. immitis infections detected in MWD during post‐mission screening using a quantitative risk analysis approach. Scenario trees were developed to describe the sequences of events leading to the return of an infected dog from a mission abroad, accounting for parasite biology, prophylactic measures, and compliance. The model estimated a mean annual number of 4.25 infected MWD returning from missions out of an average annual population of 466 returning dogs, of which 79% were detected through post‐mission screening. Most infections were likely acquired before deployment, either during previous missions, at the breeding facility before purchase, or within mainland France. Only 7.9% of infections acquired during missions were expected to be detected by testing performed at the end of the post‐mission quarantine period. Alternative scenarios highlighted the effectiveness of chemoprophylaxis, as its absence was associated with a 3.2‐fold increase in the number of infected dogs. Simulations also showed that extending the interval between return and testing would substantially improve the detection of mission‐acquired infections. These findings support the continued use of preventive measures while questioning the adequacy of current post‐mission screening alone for identifying D. immitis infections acquired during deployment.

papers.title: Natural Is Not Necessarily Safer: A Probabilistic Assessment of Risk–Risk Trade‐Offs Between Cardiovascular and Genotoxic Effects of Food Preservatives
papers.abstract: To extend product shelf life, it is especially important to prevent foods from deteriorating. Apart from the traditional methods of adding salt or sugar in large amounts, other additives, such as food preservatives, can also be applied to achieve the aim of food preservation. This study employs probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) to quantify human health impacts associated with exposure to sodium chloride, sucrose, benzoic acid (BA), and sorbic acid (SA), utilizing cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevalence and micronuclei (MN) induction frequency as dual epidemiological and toxicological endpoints. We evaluated the risks of natural and artificial preservatives in products, such as pickled vegetables, fermented vegetables, candied fruits, and preserved fruits, with the same antibacterial efficiency and under controlled pH and water activity conditions. The results revealed a significant risk trade‐off: Although the CVD prevalence associated with natural preservatives reached 16.2%–18.2% across different food categories, the MN frequency induced by artificial preservatives remained comparatively lower at 7.4%–11.6%. The results suggest that combining natural and artificial preservatives may reduce sodium chloride or sucrose intake and the associated cardiovascular health risks compared with using natural preservatives alone. These findings indicate that although limiting high‐sodium and high‐sugar foods is crucial for cardiovascular health, dietary exposure to artificial preservatives, such as BA and SA, was associated with relatively low estimated genotoxic risks, though potential hepatic or renal impacts warrant further investigation.

papers.title: Anticipating Surprises by Expanding a Risk Assessment's Possibility Space Into the Unknown With C – K Theory
papers.abstract: What should a risk assessor do if she suspects the possibilities derivable from presently available knowledge are incomplete? Risk analysts often encounter this problem when assessing risk in open systems that produce novel outcomes leading to surprises. The solution is to expand the possibility space into the unknown. Yet the novel possibilities then included cannot be mere figments of the imagination; they must be tethered to presently available knowledge to be credible. This may seem paradoxical: to go beyond presently available knowledge by assessing novel possibilities, which, to be credible, must be grounded in presently available knowledge. Yet it is not quite as contradictory as it may first seem. C – K Theory (CKT) was developed to explain how innovators overcome a similar problem when designing a new product. An innovation involves creating something that has novel features. Some of its components may, therefore, not yet exist, and there may even be uncertainty about whether they are technically feasible. This lack of knowledge makes it difficult to determine the innovation's possibility space—a difficulty similar to that faced when assessing risks in open systems. CKT describes how innovators overcome this problem by iteratively moving between a knowledge space comprising established facts and decidable propositions and a conceptual space representing novel, as‐yet‐undecidable propositions. As illustrated herein using the cases of the credit crunch and the 9/11 terrorist attack, CKT can help anticipate surprises by generating, expanding, and integrating the possibility space within the extended ( C , U ) risk‐assessment framework.

papers.title: Forecasting LLM‐Enabled Biorisk and the Efficacy of Safeguards
papers.abstract: Capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on several biological benchmarks have prompted not only excitement about their usefulness for research but also concern about biosecurity risks. We recruited 46 subject‐matter experts in biology and biosecurity, and 22 generalist forecasters to estimate the risks of growing LLM capabilities. Most respondents expected some hypothetical LLM capabilities to increase their estimates of risk and dramatically underestimated the rate of LLM progress in those capabilities. When these capabilities arose, the median forecast did update as anticipated. The median expert initially predicted a 0.3% annual risk of a human‐caused epidemic that causes 100,000 deaths. This estimate then rose to 1.5% conditional on several hypothetical LLM capabilities, including matching the performance of a top‐performing team of virologists on a virology troubleshooting test, which the median expert did not expect to occur until 2030. Given this finding, we conducted a baselining study and found that LLMs already crossed this performance threshold in April 2025. A follow‐up survey conducted after these results were available found that forecasters significantly updated their median unconditional risk estimates upward, with the new median expert forecast of annual risk rising to 1.5% (as anticipated by the earlier conditional forecasts). More encouragingly, most experts thought that the adoption of LLM safeguards and mandatory nucleic acid screening would negate the risk associated with some hypothetical LLM capabilities.

papers.title: Assessment of Risks, Efficiency, Costs, and Gain of Natural Hazard (Catastrophe) Consequences Prevention Based on Geophysical Monitoring
papers.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to quantitatively estimate the efficiency of forecasting hazards and catastrophic processes induced by high‐energy terrestrial sources, based on an integrated monitoring of the state of geophysical processes. Using methods of mathematical statistics and detection theory, relations have been obtained that can be used to calculate the coefficients of the efficiency of warning of catastrophes and the costs associated with a predicted event. The hazard (catastrophe) prevention efficiency coefficient has been shown to be dependent only on the conditional probability of missing a hazard. The relative cost parameter is a function of five parameters: a priori probability of the unwanted event, a conditional false alarm probability, a conditional missed detect probability, relative costs in the case of false alarm probability, and costs to minimize consequences of the hazardous event in case it has been accurately forecast. The gain from organizing geophysical monitoring has been estimated for a few dangers and catastrophes of terrestrial nature. The gain has been shown to be significant in many cases. An energy‐based classification of the most important natural sources of hazards and catastrophes, as well as their consequences, is proposed or improved.

papers.title: An Agent‐Based Model for Post‐Disaster Resource Allocation Considering Dynamic Demand
papers.abstract: In the response phase of a disaster, effective and equitable resource allocation is critical for meeting the needs of affected populations and maintaining the social order in disaster‐stricken areas. However, dynamic demand driven by the mobility of disaster‐affected populations can substantially impact resource allocation outcomes. To consider this mobility in the resource allocation problem, in this paper, we employ an agent‐based model to simulate cross‐shelter movements and assess the performance of resource allocation strategies considering a gradual increase of total available resources over time. A novel resource allocation strategy is proposed, which leverages demand estimation through a machine learning (ML) method‐XGBoost. We then compare this approach against two conventional strategies: uniform distribution and historical data averaging. Through case studies using real‐world data of Typhoon Ragasa from Shenzhen in China and Lal‐lo in the Philippines, we demonstrate that our proposed strategy comprehensively outperforms the other two in terms of effectiveness, equity and stability. In conclusion, this ML‐based prediction approach offers valuable insights to support decision‐makers in the formulation of resource allocation plans.

papers.title: Systemic Risk Revisited: A Working Definition and Diagnostic Framework for Risk Analysis
papers.abstract: Systemic risk has gained increasing attention across disaster risk reduction, climate governance, finance, infrastructure, and other domains, yet its meaning and application remain inconsistent. Existing definitions emphasize interdependence, contagion, complexity, uncertainty, cascading effects, and system‐wide disruption, but differ in analytical focus and operational use. This paper reviews major definitional traditions and argues that a working definition and diagnostic framework can clarify the analytical basis of systemic risk. We define systemic risk as potential damage, loss, and impact that propagate through interdependencies, feedbacks, and nonlinear processes within or across interconnected systems. Building on this definition, the paper develops a diagnostic framework based on system structure, propagation pathways, dynamic mechanisms, and cascading consequences. These dimensions help distinguish systemic risks from risks that are severe, complex, or large scale but remain relatively contained, and provide a structured basis for examining how adverse consequences propagate within and across interconnected systems in different domains.

papers.title: Information Spillovers Across Media Markets: Risk Perceptions and Cyclospora Outbreaks in U.S. Bagged Salads
papers.abstract: From 2018 to 2022, contamination of fresh produce by Cyclospora cayetanensis , primarily affecting bagged salads, caused more than 3,300 outbreak‐associated illnesses across the United States. Yet the economic consequences of these outbreaks, and the role of information exposure in shaping consumer responses, remain poorly understood. This study quantifies changes in bagged salad purchases and associated retail losses during six selected large multistate outbreaks occurring from 2018 to 2022 and examines how risk perceptions evolve across outbreak‐affected and neighboring regions. Guided by a risk perception framework emphasizing risk proximity and information‐driven belief updating, we integrate epidemiologic outbreak data, designated market area (DMA)‐level Google Trends search intensity as a geographically granular proxy for information exposure, and NielsenIQ household purchase data. Because DMAs often cross state lines, this design identifies information spillovers to non‐outbreak states sharing a media market. A Heckman selection framework accounts for purchase participation and unobserved heterogeneity, while complementary retail scanner data assess whether retailer stocking adjustments contributed to the observed purchase declines. Across the outbreak periods examined in this study, weekly bagged salad purchases declined by an average of 3.89%, implying cumulative retail losses of approximately $373.67 million. Outbreak‐specific searches (e.g., “Cyclospora”) were associated with greater perceived risk and larger purchase reductions, while general salad‐related searches were associated with smaller reductions. Spillovers across shared media markets further reduced purchases in non‐outbreak states by 3.33% per week. Retailer analysis found no statistically significant store‐level stocking reductions during outbreak or recall periods, supporting the interpretation that the observed purchase declines were primarily demand‐driven. These findings highlight the economic significance of information‐driven consumer responses and the importance of timely, accurate, and geographically targeted risk communication during foodborne outbreaks.

papers.title: Toward Understanding Implications of AI‐Powered Intelligent Transportation Systems on Risk Research and Practice
papers.abstract: The rapidly evolving use of artificial intelligence (AI)‐powered intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and other emerging technologies in the transportation sector has the potential to deliver unprecedented improvements in safety and efficiency. However, recent research has also raised concerns about the implications of using AI and automation, as these technologies can introduce new, understudied risks to such systems. This perspective article evaluates AI‐powered ITS through three lenses: risk assessment, concerning whether current conceptual and methodological tools remain sufficient for these systems; the human element, relating to how analysts and operators interact with AI outputs, including explainable AI (XAI) and human‐in‐the‐loop oversight; and governance, concerning frameworks needed to manage these systems. Across these lenses, the article uses risk characterization as a diagnostic tool for locating where established risk practice must adapt and translates the resulting gaps into specific research directions. Although the practical interpretation and application of fundamental risk concepts may change when viewed through the lens of AI‐powered ITS, the work of this article provides a basis for research directions and requirements needed for risk practice to adapt to new and emerging technologies and to support future research and training within the risk analysis community. This perspective will be of interest to risk researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

papers.title: Human Development and the Architecture of Everyday Worry: Latent Worry Profiles in the World Risk Poll
papers.abstract: Whether public concern about risk rises or falls with national development has been debated for three decades, but the debate has compared countries hazard by hazard, asking how much people worry rather than how worry is organized. We provide a person‐centered analysis of everyday worry at global scale, applying latent class analysis to the six‐hazard worry battery of the Lloyd's Register Foundation World Risk Poll and linking profiles to the Human Development Index (HDI) in 140 countries (; 2023 wave), with the 2021 wave (; 119 countries) as an independent replication. Four worry profiles replicate almost exactly across waves, including a configurationally distinct secure‐basics profile (15% of respondents) combining low worry about food and water with high worry about crime, severe weather, and traffic. Profile prevalence is consistent with the ordered sequence predicted by a need‐priority account of worry allocation: pervasive worry falls from 33% to 13% between low‐ and very‐high‐HDI countries, low worry nearly doubles, and the secure‐basics profile holds steady across low‐ and medium‐HDI countries before declining at higher development. Traffic accidents are the most intense worry in every tier below very high HDI. These gradients persist after adjustment for self‐reported recent harm and demographic composition and are only partly accounted for by the objective hazard environment, though the cross‐sectional design cannot separate development from macroregional clustering. Development is associated with the composition of worry, not only its overall level; risk communication may be better matched to a country's worry architecture than to a single global template.

papers.title: Comparing Like With Like in Biological Invasion Risk Analysis
papers.abstract: Biological invasion decision‐support methods are often compared under broad labels such as “risk assessment,” even when they perform different functions. This Perspective argues that functional commensurability must be established before methods are compared. In biological invasion risk analysis, screening serves an initial risk identification function, flagging extant or horizon non‐native species within a defined risk assessment area for prevention, surveillance, or more detailed evaluation. Comprehensive risk assessment examines entry or introduction, establishment, spread, and their ecological, economic, and socio‐cultural consequences in greater detail. Risk management integrates risk with feasibility, cost, effectiveness, legal constraints, and stakeholder values. Impact classification and post‐establishment population prioritization may contribute to these functions without being equivalent to them. Published comparisons show how conflating such functions can create false equivalence. The emerging Dispersal‐Origin‐Status‐Impact (DOSI) literature provides an illustrative example through its comparisons with applications of the globally implemented Invasiveness Screening Kit (ISK) decision‐support tools: population status and management priority are not the same quantities as prospective invasion risk screening, and species‐based screening does not imply coarse spatial resolution. Forty‐five peer‐reviewed ISK‐family studies report local or subnational screenings, including spatial resolutions comparable with or finer than DOSI applications. Valid comparisons require a shared decision objective, explicit spatial and temporal boundaries, independent evaluation evidence, and assessment of uncertainty and the consequences of error. These requirements permit methods to be evaluated for a common use, or combined within adaptive management, without treating disagreement between unlike outputs as evidence of superior performance.

papers.title: An Integrated Risk‐Informed Optimization Framework for Disinformation Interdiction in Coupled Information‐Physical Networks
papers.abstract: The manner in which society consumes and responds to information has significantly evolved in recent years, increasing the potential risk of interacting with, reacting to, and spreading misinformation and disinformation. In this paper, we introduce a novel integrated optimization framework that simultaneously models the dynamics of an information layer (where correct information or false information spreads) and a physical layer (where users interact with a physical infrastructure system). We consider an over‐the‐horizon problem in which an adversary seeks to disrupt physical infrastructure by spreading false information about its operation and performance, prompting users to behave in ways that degrade system performance. Focusing on public transit, we study how disinformation about station closures alters user behavior and system efficiency, and develop an optimization model to identify effective interdiction strategies that mitigate these impacts. The information layer incorporates personality‐driven susceptibility and simulates dis/information diffusion, while the physical layer uses a multicommodity network flow model to capture user movements and expose the effects of disinformation on travel time. Our integrated approach enables the joint analysis of both layers, revealing complex interdependencies that are overlooked when studied separately. A case study of the New York City subway system shows that even limited protective interventions can significantly reduce travel delays. In contrast, unmitigated disinformation can substantially degrade system performance. This research highlights the importance of integrated optimization‐based strategies for enhancing the resilience of transportation systems to information‐based threats and provides a foundation for future studies on dynamic disinformation influence on physical infrastructure systems.

papers.title: Risk Assessment of an Illegal Laboratory in Reedley, California, Using Geospatial Analysis of Open‐Source Epidemic Intelligence Data
papers.abstract: An illegal laboratory discovered in Reedley, California, in December 2022 was in a warehouse, operating without a license, handling about a thousand transgenic mice, chemicals, and possibly over 20 pathogens, including vials labeled Ebola, which were never tested but destroyed. This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open‐source epidemic intelligence data. We utilized data from EPIWATCH, from October 2021 to October 2023, a year prior to and a year after the establishment of the illegal laboratory. The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. In California, an upward trend in outbreak signals of pathogens associated with the laboratory was noted in December 2022, April 2023, and August 2023. In the hotspot analysis, California and eight other states in the United States (US) were identified as hotspots. Narrative evidence revealed the presence of a sick employee working in the laboratory, whose child also became ill. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. A subsequent illegal lab linked to Reedley was identified in Las Vegas in 2026, highlighting the ongoing threat to biosecurity. EPIWATCH geospatial and temporal analysis can enhance the public health risk assessment of threats associated with illegal laboratories, especially when there is no available testing or reporting.

papers.title: Modeling Exposure–Mortality Relationships for Indoor Heat
papers.abstract: Most individuals spend the majority of their time indoors. However, epidemiological evidence of the association between heat and mortality is dominated by studies using outdoor temperature as a proxy for personal exposure. To demonstrate how an exposure–response relationship between indoor heat and mortality may relate to that between outdoor heat and mortality, we develop a novel mathematical modeling approach. This approachuses the relationship between regional daily average indoor and outdoor temperature to map the exposure–response relationship for outdoor heat, estimated by epidemiological studies, to indoor heat. Due to the modifying effect of buildings on heat exposure, we show that a change in indoor temperature may be associated with a greater change in mortality than an equal change in outdoor temperature. This has implications for researchers seeking to assess the health impact of changes in indoor heat exposure. Furthermore, it provides a new theoretical framework for interpreting potential differences in the temperature‐mortality relationship of indoor and outdoor heat exposure in epidemiological studies.

papers.title: Seasonal Multivariate and Spatial Assessment of Heavy Metal Contamination and Associated Ecotoxicological and Human Health Risks in Urban Park Soils: A Case Study From Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam
papers.abstract: Urban parks in rapidly developing cities face increasing heavy metal contamination, yet seasonal dynamics remain poorly understood. This study evaluated seasonal variations in heavy metal contamination and associated human health risks in two major parks in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. We analyzed 48 surface soil samples (24 locations × 2 seasons) for eight metals using ICP‐OES. Pollution levels were evaluated using indices (EF, I geo , CF, PER, mHQ, TU, and TRI) and GIS‐geostatistics. Sources were apportioned via multivariate analysis and positive matrix factorization (PMF), and health risks to children and adults were simulated using Monte Carlo methods. Al (Go Vap 12,475 ppm; Gia Dinh 13,998 ppm) and Fe (Go Vap 12,324.1 ppm; Gia Dinh 7620.7 ppm) dominated soil composition. In Go Vap, there was an increase in Al, Mn enrichment and Pb spikes (EF = 91.69) in the dry season; Gia Dinh had Cr (EF = 4.43) enrichment in the dry season and higher Mn (EF = 4.19) in the rainy season. PMF identified four sources: traffic solid waste (31.4%), traffic emissions and construction dust (15.8%), natural weathering (20.1%), and redox processes (32.7%). Spatial analysis revealed dry‐season high‐risk hotspots expanding to 39.41% of Gia Dinh and 36.02% of Go Vap park areas. Cr posed the highest health risk (HQ = 0.53 for children, 0.057 for adults), primarily via ingestion. All risk indices intensified during the dry season ( p < 0.05). Dry seasons increase the risk of contamination in tropical urban parks, especially Cr. This study supports seasonal monitoring and enhanced protection for children in monsoon‐affected green spaces.

papers.title: Modeling Logical Interdependencies: Quantifying Systemic Risk From Rule‐Governed Actions
papers.abstract: Systemic risk in critical infrastructure is often analyzed through physical, geographic, and cyber interdependencies. Yet infrastructures are also interdependent through the governing rules that organize human action. These rule‐mediated connections are a form of logical interdependency, and breakdowns in rule‐governed action can create pathways through which disruption spreads. This paper develops a framework for diagnosing and quantifying this underrecognized source of systemic risk. It does so by modeling logical interdependencies as rule‐mediated control relations that shape whether interconnected infrastructures remain within safe operating bounds or drift toward failure. Integrating Institutional Grammar, STAMP, and Bayesian inference, the framework translates governing rules into structured control relations, represents them within a socio‐technical control architecture, and quantifies how failures in those relations propagate across interconnected infrastructures. We demonstrate the framework through a reservoir system case study centered on Lake Mendocino, California, where safety depends not only on reservoir infrastructure and hydrologic conditions, but also on distributed authority, communication requirements, and operational protocols. The results show that logical interdependencies make non‐trivial contributions to modeled systemic risk, with baseline probabilities of 7% for Coyote Valley Dam failure and 3% for downstream community impacts under the modeled conditions. More importantly, the analysis reveals hidden logical risk : rules and control relations that appear routine in normal operation yet become disproportionately important when the Bayesian model traces which factors most strongly contribute to a failure scenario. The paper moves logical interdependencies from a residual conceptual category to a systematically identifiable and quantitatively analyzable pathway of systemic risk.

papers.title: Inseparability in Disaster Risk Science: Accounting for Coupled, Co‐Evolving Systems
papers.abstract: Contemporary risk landscapes are shaped by systemic phenomena—compound disasters, cascading failures, non‐stationarity, and cross‐domain crises—that challenge conventional frameworks. While the classical risk equation (Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure) remains a useful heuristic, it relies on a separability assumption that breaks down in feedback‐rich, co‐evolving systems. This failure reflects a familiar diagnosis: risk can be mistaken for a complicated problem, decomposable and optimizable, when it is a complex one, characterized by emergence and adaptation. Our contribution herein is not this distinction but its analytical consequence. Drawing on an interdisciplinary workshop on systemic risk and resilience, we propose inseparability as a foundational premise for disaster risk science. Hazard, exposure, and vulnerability might be better understood as dynamically coupled processes rather than separable variables. We derive implications across four axes: reframing vulnerability as a non‐ergodic system property; addressing cross‐scale dynamics; shifting from risk control to adaptive management; and treating knowledge co‐production as a scientific necessity.

papers.title: Ambient Air Pollution Health Impacts in High‐Income Countries, Part II: A Case Study in the United Arab Emirates
papers.abstract: Ambient air pollution poses major global public health risks, particularly in rapidly developing regions, including the Arabian Gulf. This study estimates the disease burden attributable to anthropogenic air pollution (particulate matter [PM] and ozone) in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, for 2019–2022 and compares findings to previous estimates for 2008. Burdens were calculated using updated air quality, population, and health incidence data for 2019–2022 along with concentration–response functions from recent epidemiologic evidence. Results show that Abu Dhabi's investments in air quality management have paid off in preventing air quality from deteriorating as much as would be expected given the doubling of the population between 2008 and 2022. However, epidemiologic evidence gathered during this period indicates that PM exposure has stronger negative effects on mortality risks than previously thought. As a result, estimated deaths attributable to anthropogenic ambient air pollution increased between 2008 and 2022, from 231 (90% uncertainty interval [UI]: 59–427) to 1249 (90% UI: 507–2169). Total hospital visits attributable to PM and ozone exposure also increased. These increases reflect combined effects of population growth, higher pollutant exposures, improved medical record‐keeping, and updated evidence on health risks. Urban centers, with higher pollutant concentrations and population densities, experience the highest risks, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to address air pollution hotspots. This work provides policymakers with up‐to‐date insights on the health impacts of ambient air pollution and underscores the importance of continued investments in air quality management in Abu Dhabi.

papers.title: Enterprise Architecture Threat Modeling for Cybersecurity Risk Management
papers.abstract: Organizations invest heavily in cybersecurity capabilities, yet the relationship between deployed defensive portfolios, practitioner judgments of coverage, and empirically observed adversary behavior remains difficult to assess. This study examines that relationship by integrating practitioner elicitation with threat‐informed cybersecurity architecture analysis. A model‐derived analytical baseline was constructed using the Cybersecurity Architecture Review (CAR) methodology aligned with MITRE ATT&CK version 17, quantifying protect, detect, and respond coverage for 12 commonly deployed cybersecurity capability categories. Survey data from 65 cybersecurity practitioners were used to characterize capability portfolios, perceived coverage, and factors influencing capability‐selection decisions. Results show uneven modeled coverage across the ATT&CK lifecycle and substantial functional overlap among capability categories. Across 910 respondent‐tactic observations, practitioner‐estimated coverage exceeded corresponding respondent‐specific modeled coverage by approximately 27 percentage points on average, although the magnitude and direction of perception‐model divergence varied by tactic. Most subgroup comparisons by professional role, responsibility, and experience did not identify statistically significant differences, while government respondents exhibited slightly higher mean divergence than nongovernment respondents in one pairwise comparison. Capability‐selection decisions reflected multiple organizational and external influences, with formal internal threat modeling reported less frequently than peer practices, regulatory or compliance requirements, independent research, and analyst or consultant reports. The findings demonstrate how threat‐informed architecture analysis can complement practitioner judgment by making modeled coverage, gaps, overlap, and divergence explicit within organizational cybersecurity risk governance.

papers.title: AccES: A Framework for Predicting Building‐Level Loss of Accessibility to Essential Services Post‐Disasters Based on Publicly Available Information
papers.abstract: Natural hazards significantly disrupt access to essential services, affecting individuals' capacity to withstand and recover from such events. However, existing hazard resilience models often fail to account for the interdependencies among essential services and lack the spatial resolution needed to assess accessibility loss at the building level. This study introduces the Predicting Loss of Access to Essential Services (AccES) framework—a novel, data‐driven, and people‐centered approach that uses publicly available information to evaluate accessibility following a natural hazard event. The framework integrates open‐source datasets with local stakeholder knowledge to develop spatially explicit models of interconnected infrastructure networks, including power, water, and communication networks, along with their dependent service facilities such as hospitals, childcare centers, and grocery stores. Accessibility loss is assessed by evaluating the disruptions to infrastructure networks and service facilities, estimating (1) the probability that individual buildings lose access to infrastructure services and (2) the expected increase in travel distance to the nearest operational service facility. To demonstrate the framework's utility, a case study was conducted in Cayey, Puerto Rico, simulating the impacts of a Category 2 tropical cyclone. Results highlight spatial disparities in accessibility loss, with rural and socially vulnerable areas facing greater burdens. AccES advances hazard resilience modeling by providing a scalable, equity‐oriented tool to support data‐informed decision‐making for both pre‐disaster planning and post‐disaster response.

papers.title: Interactions Among Three‐Tier Factors of Community Safety Resilience: A Dual‐Perspective Analysis
papers.abstract: Enhancing community safety resilience (CSR) is critical for sustainable urban development. Disregarding the complex interactions among CSR factors may cause imbalanced resilience building, limiting a community's capacity to respond to uncertain disasters. This study aims to identify principal CSR factors and examine their interaction mechanisms in the context of Chinese urban communities. We identified 101 factors spanning government, community, and personal tiers. Their interactions were assessed via expert elicitation and analyzed using directed weighted network theory and a modified susceptible‐infectious‐recovered model. The factor interaction network exhibits a sparse, highly modular, core‐periphery structure with small‐world and scale‐free properties. Community‐level governance and infrastructure, together with personal‐level physiological and psychological factors, serve as both hubs and intermediary bridges. Government‐level top‐level design, organizational leadership, and support and investment act as primary drivers, critical in initiating and mitigating risk propagation. Fundamental risk mitigation, especially under dual perturbations, depends on government action, whereas community‐level factors are vital for localized response. These findings provide an analytical foundation for prioritizing interventions and designing system‐sensitive strategies to enhance CSR.

papers.title: The Distinct Roles of Anger and Hope in PFAS Risk Processing: Integrating Mixed Emotional Appeals and Efficacy Information into the EPPM
papers.abstract: Guided by the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), this study examines the distinct persuasive mechanisms of mixed emotional appeals and efficacy information in the context of environmental risk communication (per‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances, PFAS). Results of a 3 (emotional appeals: fear/fear + anger/fear + hope) × 2 (efficacy information: low/high) between‐subjects experiment ( N = 405) in China revealed that adding anger to fear appeals significantly increased perceived threat, whereas adding hope enhanced perceived self‐efficacy. Although providing high‐efficacy information enhanced perceived efficacy, it led to a minor reduction in perceived threat. Notably, the interaction analyses showed that high‐efficacy information increased response efficacy most strongly in the fear + anger condition. In contrast, fear + hope appeals enhanced self‐efficacy even when efficacy information was low. Furthermore, only perceived threat and response efficacy emerged as significant predictors of preventive behaviors. Theoretical implications for expanding the EPPM to include mixed emotions and practical implications for designing PFAS risk messages are discussed.
